configuration options. ::properties ::property name: 'apikey', type: 'string' your api authentication key. required for all requests. ::property name: 'timeout', type: 'integer' request timeout in milliseconds. defaults to 30000. ::property name: 'retries', type: 'integer' number of retry attempts for failed requests. defaults to 3. ::property name: 'debug', type: 'boolean' enable debug logging for troubleshooting. defaults to false. :: usage: --- layout columns id: 'layout-columns' create multi-column layouts for side-by-side content. ::row ::col left column this content appears in the left title: Authentication
description: In this guide, we'll look at how authentication works. Protocol offers two ways to authenticate your API requests: Basic authentication and OAuth2 with a token.
content: authentication you'll need to authenticate your requests to access any of the endpoints in the protocol api. in this guide, we'll look at how authentication works. protocol offers two ways to authenticate your api requests: basic authentication and oauth2 with a token — oauth2 is the recommended way. classname: 'lead' basic authentication with basic authentication, you use your username and password to authenticate your http requests. unless you have a very good reason, you probably shouldn't use basic auth. here's how to authenticate using curl: please don't commit your protocol password to github! oauth2 with bearer token the recommended way to authenticate with the protocol api is by using oauth2. when establishing a connection using oauth2, you will need your access token — you will find it in the protocol dashboard under api settings. here's how to add the token to the request header using curl: always keep your token safe and reset it if you suspect it has been compromised. using an sdk if you use one of our official sdks, you won't have to worry about any of the above — fetch your access token from the protocol dashboard under api settings, and the client library will take care of the rest. all the client libraries use oauth2 behind the scenes. ::button url: '/sdks', variant: 'text' check out our list of first-party sdks ::icon arrow-right ::

title: Pagination
description: In this guide, we will look at how to work with paginated responses when querying the Protocol API
content: pagination in this guide, we will look at how to work with paginated responses when querying the protocol api. by default, all responses limit results to ten. however, you can go as high as 100 by adding a parameter to your requests. if you are using one of the official protocol api client libraries, you don't need to worry about pagination, as it's all being taken care of behind the scenes. classname: 'lead' when an api response returns a list of objects, no matter the amount, pagination is supported. in paginated responses, objects are nested in a attribute and have a attribute that indicates whether you have reached the end of the last page. you can use the and query parameters to browse pages. example using cursors ::row ::col in this example, we request the page that starts after the conversation with id . as a result, we get a list of three conversations and can tell by the attribute that we have reached the end of the resultset. ::properties ::property name: 'startingafter', type: 'string' the last id on the page you're currently on when you want to fetch the next page. ::property name: 'endingbefore', type: 'string' the first id on the page you're currently on when you want to fetch the previous page. ::property name: 'limit', type: 'integer' limit the number of items returned. :: ::col ::

title: Errors
description: In this guide, we will talk about what happens when something goes wrong while you work with the API.
content: errors in this guide, we will talk about what happens when something goes wrong while you work with the api. mistakes happen, and mostly they will be yours, not ours. let's look at some status codes and error types you might encounter. classname: 'lead' you can tell if your request was successful by checking the status code when receiving an api response. if a response comes back unsuccessful, you can use the error type and error message to figure out what has gone wrong and do some rudimentary debugging before contacting support. ::callout before reaching out to support with an error, please be aware that 99% of all reported errors are, in fact, user errors. therefore, please carefully check your code before contacting protocol support. :: error types ::row ::col whenever a request is unsuccessful, the protocol api will return an error response with an error type and message. you can use this information to understand better what has gone wrong and how to fix it. most of the error messages are pretty helpful and actionable. here is a list of the two error types supported by the protocol api — use these to understand what you have done wrong. ::properties ::property name: 'apierror' this means that we made an error, which is highly speculative and unlikely. ::property name: 'invalidrequest' this means that you made an error, which is much more likely. :: ::col ::

title: Installation Guide
description: Complete step-by-step guide for installing NoMercy.
content: installation requirements before installing nomercy, ensure your system meets the following requirements: - operating system: windows 10+, macos 10.12+, or linux ubuntu 20.04+ recommended - memory: minimum 4gb ram 8gb recommended - storage: at least 10gb free space for application and database - network: stable internet connection for initial setup installation steps 1. download nomercy visit the official nomercy github repository and download the latest release suitable for your operating system. 2. extract files extract the downloaded archive to your preferred installation directory: 3. run installation script execute the installation script appropriate for your system: 4. configure basic settings during installation, you'll be prompted to: - set the installation directory - configure database connection - set up initial admin account - configure media storage paths 5. start the service after installation, start the nomercy service: verification to verify successful installation, access the nomercy web interface: - url: http://localhost:7000 default - admin account: use the credentials you created during installation next steps once installed: 1. configure mediaserver - set up media storage 2. add content - start adding your entertainment files 3. access the web interface to begin organizing your library troubleshooting if you encounter installation issues: - check that your system meets the minimum requirements - ensure all required ports are available default: 7000, 7001 - review the installation logs in the directory - consult the faq or open an issue on github getting help for additional support: - visit the nomercy documentation - check out the mediaserver guide - open an issue on the github repository

title: MediaServer Overview
description: Comprehensive overview of NoMercy MediaServer component.
content: what is mediaserver? mediaserver is a core component of nomercy that handles media file storage, organization, and streaming. it provides efficient management of your entertainment content library with powerful indexing and search capabilities. key features media organization - automatic cataloging: automatically detect and categorize media files - smart tagging: intelligent tagging system for content discovery - folder structure: flexible organization supporting complex folder hierarchies - multi-format support: support for various video, audio, and image formats streaming capabilities - direct streaming: stream media directly to supported devices - format transcoding: automatic transcoding for optimal playback quality - adaptive bitrate: intelligent bitrate adjustment for different connection speeds - subtitle support: automatic subtitle detection and management performance & reliability - efficient indexing: fast indexing for quick content discovery - caching system: intelligent caching for improved performance - backup support: built-in backup and recovery mechanisms - monitoring: real-time monitoring of media library health supported media formats video formats - mp4, mkv, avi, mov, flv, webm, and more audio formats - mp3, flac, aac, ogg, wav, and more image formats - jpg, png, webp, gif, and more components mediaserver consists of several components: 1. indexer: scans and catalogs media files 2. database: stores metadata and configuration 3. streamer: handles media playback and delivery 4. monitor: tracks system health and performance getting started with mediaserver to get started with mediaserver: 1. configure mediaserver - set up paths and settings 2. add media folders to your library 3. let the indexer scan and organize your content 4. start streaming and enjoying your media next steps - configuration guide - detailed setup instructions - nomercy getting started - return to main guide - installation guide - complete installation reference

title: MediaServer Configuration
description: How to configure NoMercy MediaServer using startup flags, environment variables, and the in-app web UI.
content: there is no config file nomercy mediaserver has no configuration file. there is no , , , or file to edit. settings are controlled in two places: - startup flags or environment variables — port, ip address, log level, and a few launch-time options - web ui — everything else: libraries, users, encoder settings, and general preferences open after the server starts to reach the dashboard. environment variables every flag has a matching environment variable. environment variables are applied when the corresponding flag is not passed. this is the primary way to configure docker deployments. | variable | equivalent flag | example | |:--|:--|:--| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | --- docker: the hostip requirement when running in docker, the container cannot auto-detect your host machine's lan ip. you must supply it via the environment variable, which the provided compose files map from a shell variable. the compose file contains: if you skip this step, the server starts but clients on other devices may not be able to discover or connect to it. you can also hard-code the value directly in the compose file instead of using the shell variable. for gpu-accelerated transcoding, use the matching compose variant: --- adding libraries via the web ui after first login, add your media libraries through the web dashboard. navigate to settings > libraries, then click add library. choose the library type movies, tv shows, or music, give it a name, and select the folder path where your media files live. the server will begin scanning immediately. library paths must be accessible to the server process. for docker, this means the folder must be mounted as a volume in your compose file. the provided compose template includes commented-out volume entries under , , and — uncomment and adjust those paths to match your actual media locations before starting the container. --- port forwarding to access your server from outside your home network, forward port or whichever port you configured on your router to your server's lan ip. once a certificate is issued during first-run setup, the server uses https automatically. --- next steps - title: What is the Music Player
description: The headless audio engine with sample-accurate crossfade, what it does and where it sits.
content: what is the nomercy music player is the headless audio engine that powers music on nomercy tv. the tricky part of a music player is the hand-off between two tracks, and this engine is built around getting it right: sample-accurate crossfade on the web audio backend, or a gapless transition when you want one track to run straight into the next. lyric sync and a full eq chain are here too. no ui is bundled; you wire your own to plain events and methods. what you get - , a typed player class generic over your own track type - , a factory that creates or returns a named instance - sample-accurate crossfade and gapless playback, with a swappable audio backend - lyric sync, a ten-band equalizer, and spectrum data for visualisers - a plugin for every optional capability, plus full typescript types where it sits the generic parts queue, auth, plugins, i18n, storage live in underneath, so this package stays focused on what makes audio hard. .' , n: 1, name: 'nomercy-player-core', pkg: 'peer dependency', knows: 'queue, auth, plugins, event bus, i18n, storage.' , /> next steps - quick start: a working player in a few lines - configuration: every option and default - crossfade: the signature feature - architecture: the web audio signal chain, the equalizer, and the design decisions

title: Installation
description: Install nomercy-music-player via npm, yarn, or pnpm. Requirements and import paths.
content: installation requirements - node.js 18 or later tooling only, the player itself runs in any modern browser - a module bundler vite, webpack, rollup, or similar install the package the package-manager toggle, pinned to the top right, switches this command to yarn, pnpm, or bun. cdn no bundler you can drop the player onto a page without a bundler. load first the iife bundle reads it from the global, then the player bundle, which exposes a global. built-in plugins are not part of the iife bundle, so use the npm install above when you need them. import paths the package ships two import paths: importing plugins from the main entry point is not supported, always use . typescript the package ships full typescript declarations. no package is needed. the recommended type for a consumer-held player reference is : use the concrete type only when you need access to internals not exposed on the interface. browser support | browser | minimum version | notes | | --------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | chrome | 90 | full support | | firefox | 90 | full support | | safari | 15 | web audio crossfade supported; native hls skips | | edge | 90 | full support | | ios safari | 15.4 | web audio may require user gesture before | | android webview | 90 | audio output routing not available | hls streams hls support is handled by . it is a production dependency of , which this package depends on, so it arrives transitively when you install . no separate install is needed. the library is loaded automatically when an url is detected on a browser that does not support native hls. on safari and ios, native hls is used directly and is not loaded. what to read next - quick start, minimal working player in under 30 lines - configuration, all options

title: Quick start
description: nomercy-music-player v2, Quick start. Copy-paste runs as-is.
content: quick start a working music player in a few lines: it loads your first track, starts playback, and surfaces system media controls lock screen, notification with the track metadata. install requires node 18+ for tooling. runs in any modern browser. minimal working player that is a working music player. the inline array is auto-queued during setup. advances the queue when a track ends. wires lock screen and notification controls. play, pause, and transport all transport methods return . they are safe to call without awaiting if you don't need to sequence work after them. queue management volume shuffle and repeat seeking listening to events see events for the full list and payload shapes. authentication if your audio sources require an header: the player injects on every hls manifest and segment request. on a 401, it calls once and retries. on a 403, the error propagates, do not retry. cdn no bundler you can drop the music player onto any page without a build step. point a at the iife bundle and you get a global. the bundle expects to be present as the global, so load that first even if you only play plain audio files. the iife bundle carries the core player only. built-in plugins media session, lyrics, equalizer, and the rest are not bundled into it, so install via npm and use esm when you need them. what to read next - configuration, all config options explained - crossfade, the signature music feature - plugin development, extend the player - events, full event reference - api methods, full method reference - recipes: crossfade & gapless, tuning crossfade for production - recipes: lyrics & equalizer, lrc sync + eq band manipulation

title: Architecture
description: How the music player is built on the player core, the Web Audio signal chain, the equalizer bands, and the key design decisions.
content: architecture the music player sits on top of the nomercy player core . the core owns: - transport lifecycle play, pause, stop, seek - queue and backlog management - plugin system and event bus - auth pipeline bearer tokens, request signing, 401 refresh - hls stream registration - cue parser registry lrc, webvtt, custom - i18n - storage adapter interface the music player adds on top of the core: - audio backends: default and - crossfade: dual-buffer crossfade with / curves - music-typed events: narrowed to , , , , , , - music plugins: , , , , , , - music adapters: , , , , , layer diagram your consumer app holds a instance, which is composed of: | part | what it provides | | ---- | ---------------- | | audio backends | or | | music plugins | , , and others | | core methods | transport, queue, auth, storage, and others | | core plugins | , , and others | key design decisions no ui in core. renders nothing. the is optional and produces a configurable dom overlay. consumers who want full control render their own ui from player events. generic playlist item. , where defaults to but consumers extend it with their own fields without wrapping or adapting. plugin-everything. lyrics, media session, cast, eq, key handling are all plugins. register only what you need. plugins are removed from the bundle via tree-shaking when not imported. backend swappable at runtime. switch between and with . custom backends inject via . what it is not - not a ui framework component no vue/react component, see framework integration - not a video player no subtitle tracks, no quality levels, see nomercy-video-player - not server-side, runs in the browser only core component responsibilities three concerns share the work of playing audio: transport and queue -- owned by the player core mixin. it drives the lifecycle state machine idle, loading, playing, paused, ended, manages the ordered playlist and backlog, handles shuffle fisher-yates and repeat modes, and serialises every operation through the event bus so plugins see consistent state. audio backends -- default wraps a single element and bridges its dom events onto the player event bus. does the same but additionally opens an , attaches a , and exposes graph mount points , for plugins. both backends implement the same contract so higher-level code never branches on which one is active. web audio signal chain -- assembled on demand by a core plugin re-exported from the music package. nothing allocates an until that plugin is registered, so playback without visualisation or eq has zero web audio overhead. web audio signal chain the baseline chain when only is active no : when is registered, it takes ownership of the chain from the backend's output node outward and manages insertion of effect nodes: the is wired in parallel to the source, not in series, so it reads the signal without interrupting the path to the speakers. > note: starts in state per the browser autoplay policy. resumes it automatically on the first event, which always fires inside a user-gesture callback. equalizer depends on and inserts a pre-gain followed by ten peaking s as effects. the band centre frequencies are: | band | frequency | | ---- | --------- | | 1 | 70 hz | | 2 | 180 hz | | 3 | 320 hz | | 4 | 600 hz | | 5 | 1,000 hz | | 6 | 3,000 hz | | 7 | 6,000 hz | | 8 | 12,000 hz | | 9 | 14,000 hz | | 10 | 16,000 hz | band gains are in the range -12 db to +12 db. index 0 is always the pre-gain pseudo-band , which maps to a at unity when set to 0. registration order matters: must be added before . spectrum analyser title: Vue Integration
description: Using NMMusicPlayer in a Vue 3 composable: reactive state, event subscriptions, and cleanup.
content: vue integration is framework-agnostic. in vue 3, wrap it in a composable to expose reactive state. composable pattern using in a component providing the player globally for apps where multiple components need the same player, provide it at the app root: pinia store pattern when several components share the same player, a pinia store is the cleanest way to centralise state and expose actions. install pinia first if it is not already in the project: wire the store at app startup: progress bar component a click-to-seek progress bar using from the store: useplayercontrols composable extract transport controls into a reusable composable so any component can call them without importing the store directly: use it in any controls component: app-level plugin / provide-inject pattern if you prefer a vue plugin over pinia, you can provide the player instance at the app root and inject it in components. this pattern suits small apps where full store infrastructure would be overkill. register it in : inject in any component: > note: is a typed symbol. prefer it over the bare string key from the "providing the player globally" example above -- it prevents key collisions in larger apps. see also - quick start, vanilla typescript setup - events, all events to bind to reactive state - react integration, same pattern for react

title: React Integration
description: Using NMMusicPlayer in a React hook: useState, useEffect, cleanup, and context pattern.
content: react integration is framework-agnostic. wrap it in a custom hook that bridges player events to component state. custom hook using in a component context pattern for apps where multiple components need the same player: error boundary react class error boundaries catch render errors. player init errors bad auth, network failure, codec problems happen inside the hook, not during render, so you need both layers. wire player-level errors from the and events in your hook, then surface them through react state so the boundary's sibling can render a recovery ui without unmounting the whole tree: performance memoize pure display components components that read queue position, current track metadata, or volume only need to re-render when those specific values change. wrap them with and pass primitive props to keep the comparison cheap: debounce high-frequency time events the event fires on every from the audio backend, which can be several times per second. do not write raw time state into react on every tick if the component only needs per-second granularity progress bars, elapsed time labels: > note: the event throttled to every 5 seconds by default is better suited for server-side watch-position saves. use only when sub-second ui updates are needed. clean up listeners to avoid leaks the player does not auto-remove listeners when a component unmounts. always return a cleanup function from . the cleanest pattern is on the player when the component that owns it unmounts; for shared instances via context remove only the listeners you added using the method: complete multi-component example this wires the context pattern, error boundary, memoized components, and debounced time into a small but complete app. tracks use the sintel and big buck bunny cc films' audio tracks as real examples. see also - quick start, vanilla typescript setup - events, all events to bind to state - vue integration, same pattern for vue 3

content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/plugins/equalizer/index.ts re-exported via music player / equalizer 10-band parametric eq provided by re-exported from the player core. import it from . the idea the equalizer is a set of tone controls you drop into the audio while it's playing. the actual audio plumbing lives in , the part that holds the and wires everything together, so you add that one first. the equalizer just hooks its ten filters into that chain, and there is nothing to shape until the chain exists, which is the whole reason for the ordering. most of the time you title: Crossfade
description: crossfadeTo(), CrossfadeOptions, automatic crossfade via AutoAdvancePlugin, and the crossfadeStart / crossfadeComplete events.
content: crossfade crossfade transitions smoothly between two tracks by fading one out while fading the other in, using a dual-buffer architecture in both built-in backends. for the full method reference see crossfade methods. how it works both backends support crossfade: - audioelementbackend: two elements; gain ramps driven by a loop ~50 fps, ±20 ms accuracy - webaudiobackend: two ramps scheduled with sample-accurate when a crossfade begins: 1. the backend loads the incoming track url into a secondary slot via 2. the secondary is pre-rolled via 3. ramps primary → 0 and secondary → volume simultaneously 4. at completion, secondary becomes primary; old primary is discarded 5. the queue cursor advances and event fires configuration set defaults that apply when no per-call options are provided: manual crossfade automatic crossfade via autoadvanceplugin calls when fires. server-triggered crossfade for radio mode, group listening, or any server-orchestrated transition: monitoring transitions backend and accuracy crossfade works with both backends. for sample-accurate transitions, use : check the active backend by , not by string comparison with the return value of : eq through crossfade during a crossfade only the outgoing track is routed through the eq graph; the incoming track plays un-equalized until it becomes the primary at the end of the fade, after which eq applies to it as normal. see also - crossfade api: , , - autoadvanceplugin: , options - events: , , - advanced: crossfade tuning: duration, curve, and timing guide - recipes: crossfade and gapless: practical walkthrough

title: Audio Backend
description: The IAudioBackend adapter: choosing between AudioElementBackend and WebAudioBackend, capabilities, crossfade accuracy, and platform constraints.
content: audio backend the audio backend is the music player's media backend adapter, the port. it is the layer between and the browser's audio apis, and it is swappable the same way every other adapter is, through the player config rather than a fork. the video player has the same role in its video backend. two implementations are built in, and you can inject your own via . the choice affects crossfade accuracy, ios compatibility, and how much web audio overhead you pay. audioelementbackend default kind: uses a native element for transport. crossfade is driven by a loop at approximately 50 fps, not sample-accurate. expect ±20 ms seams at track boundaries during a crossfade. web audio graph access is available lazily: a is created the first time a plugin requests or . you pay zero web audio overhead if no plugin requests the graph. choose this when: - running on ios where creation requires a user gesture - you need the safest possible compatibility - crossfade timing accuracy of ±20 ms is acceptable - you do not need sample-accurate crossfades but still want eq via webaudiobackend kind: routes audio through a full graph. crossfade uses for sample-accurate gain ramps. volume changes are smoothed via with a 10 ms time constant to eliminate clicks. hls streams fall back to even in mode, because requires a element. non-hls playback mp3, aac, flac, ogg also uses — the backend always routes through the element so and non-hls sources are handled identically. choose this when: - you need sample-accurate crossfades - you are building a custom audio processing chain - and are in use capability comparison | capability | | | | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | | default | yes | no | | crossfade accuracy | ~50 fps raf | sample-accurate | | eq / effect chain | via lazy mediaelementsourcenode | full audiocontext graph | | hls support | hls.js or native | hls.js or native mediaelementsource | | ios compatibility | full | requires user gesture | | output routing | yes | yes | | | yes | yes | switching at runtime switching disposes the current backend, constructs the new one, and re-wires all events. the player enters a paused state after the switch. custom backend inject a fully custom backend via in the player config: see also - title: AudioElementBackend
description: HTML5 audio element backend with lazy Web Audio graph and RAF-based crossfade, the default music player backend.
content: audioelementbackend the default audio backend. uses a native element for transport and optionally creates a when a plugin requests the web audio graph. kind: activation this backend is active by default. no configuration is required. to explicitly select it: or switch to it at runtime: hls support when the audio url ends with and the browser does not support native hls: 1. the backend imports a transitive production dependency via 2. creates an instance and calls + 3. all subsequent segment fetches are handled by on safari and ios, native hls is used directly and is skipped. web audio graph lazy the backend creates only when the first plugin calls or . until then, the element routes directly to the system output. this means and work with this backend, at a slight cost: once the is created, it cannot be removed for the lifetime of the backend instance. crossfade implementation crossfade is driven by a loop at ~50 fps. a secondary element is allocated via , pre-rolled via , and then both elements are gain-ramped in opposite directions over . - primary ramps from current volume to 0 - secondary ramps from 0 to current volume - at completion, the secondary becomes the primary element and the old primary is discarded accuracy: ±20 ms one raf frame. use for sub-millisecond accuracy. secondary gain api returns when no secondary element is allocated. output routing is available in chrome and chromium-based browsers. safari does not support it. see also - backends overview, when to choose vs - iaudiobackend, full interface reference - webaudiobackend, sample-accurate alternative

title: WebAudioBackend
description: Web Audio API pipeline backend with sample-accurate crossfade via linearRampToValueAtTime.
content: webaudiobackend web audio pipeline backend. routes all audio through a graph. crossfade uses for sample-accurate ramps. kind: activation or switch at runtime: audio graph the backend constructs a graph rooted at the : element via createmediaelementsource, for both hls and non-hls sources.' , n: 3, name: 'gainnode primary volume', pkg: 'webaudiobackend', knows: 'controls playback volume and executes crossfade ramps via linearramptovalueattime.' , n: 2, name: 'backend output node', pkg: 'webaudiobackend', knows: 'tap point for audiographplugin effect chains. connect custom analyser or effect nodes here.' , n: 1, name: 'audiocontext.destination', pkg: 'web audio api', knows: 'final sink routed to the device speakers or headphones.' , /> when is registered, it connects its effect chain between the and . source node always routes through a element and wraps it with . this applies to both hls streams and direct file urls mp3, aac, flac, ogg. attaches to the same element, so there is no separate code path per format. crossfade implementation : 1. primary ramps from current volume to 0 via 2. secondary ramps from 0 to current volume via 3. both ramps complete at 4. at completion, the secondary becomes the primary; the old primary is disconnected and its buffer released accuracy: sample-accurate. no raf loop, no jitter. volume changes are smoothed with time constant 10 ms to prevent clicks on mute/unmute or abrupt volume changes. ios considerations on ios and in some mobile chrome contexts, creation may be suspended until a user gesture. if , call inside a user interaction handler before starting playback. graph access see also - backends overview, when to choose vs - iaudiobackend, full interface reference - audioelementbackend, default, less accurate alternative - advanced: equalizer customization, building on the web audio graph

title: Playlist and Queue
description: Queue operations (append, prepend, insert, remove, shuffle, sort), peek next/prev, repeat modes, and the AutoAdvancePlugin.
content: playlist and queue queue manipulation beyond the basic call in the quickstart: inserting tracks mid-stream, a shuffle toggle, peek-ahead for preloading, or custom repeat behaviour. the queue api is identical on video and music players. examples use the music player but every method applies to both. queue basics append, prepend, and insert remove and move jump to a track peek next and previous peek is read-only, it does not change playback: shuffle when shuffle is on, returns the next shuffled item. repeat modes calls when a track ends. the player's implementation respects repeat state: when is set, it reloads and replays the current track instead of advancing the queue cursor. autoadvanceplugin drives automatic advancement when a track ends. without it, the player stops at the end of each track. sorting the queue the player does not ship a built-in sort method, so sort the array before setting it: for in-place shuffling, use fisher-yates before setting: this is a blunt replacement, but the active track is preserved because the player matches by . queue events what to read next - recipes: crossfade and gapless - smooth transitions between queue items - recipes: persistence - save and restore queue position across page loads - music, api methods - full queue method reference

title: Crossfade and Gapless
description: Music crossfade tuning, gapless transition strategy, choosing between them, and timing pitfalls.
content: crossfade and gapless smooth music transitions: a volume-faded crossfade or a preloaded gapless handoff. this applies to the music player only. prerequisites: quick start. for the full crossfade api see crossfade. crossfade vs gapless, when to choose | feature | crossfade | gapless | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | overlap | both tracks play simultaneously | tracks play sequentially | | volume | outgoing fades down, incoming fades up | constant | | use case | album transitions, radio, dj-style mixes | continuous music prog rock, live albums | | config | + | omit crossfade; preloads next | enabling crossfade with calls when fires. set to match or be less than . crossfade curve comparison keeps perceived loudness stable: use for all standard music. creates an audible dip at the midpoint, which is almost never what you want. manual crossfade trigger to crossfade on an explicit user action next button, click on a playlist item: nested crossfades are rejected by the player, so is a no-op when returns . monitoring crossfade progress gapless playback gapless preloads the next track so it can begin immediately when the current one ends: with calls when fires, so the next track's audio is buffered before . backend choice and accuracy | backend | crossfade mechanism | gapless accuracy | | --------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | | raf loop ~50 fps, ±20 ms | browser-dependent. chrome/safari good, firefox may gap | | | sample-accurate | sample-accurate on all browsers with web audio | switch to for production dj-style crossfades: timing pitfalls the crossfade seconds must be less than or equal to : see also - crossfade, full api and per-call options - autoadvanceplugin, , , and options - backends overview, vs crossfade trade-offs - lyrics and equalizer, eq applies through crossfade transitions

title: Crossfade Tuning
description: Fine-tuning crossfade duration, curves, lead time, and backend selection for different musical contexts.
content: crossfade tuning crossfade quality depends on three variables: backend choice, duration, and the lead time between the signal and when the fade starts. this page covers the trade-offs and how to tune each. backend choice determines accuracy the backend uses a loop ~50 fps. one frame is ~20 ms. gain steps are applied every frame, so transitions are not sample-accurate, and slight audible stepping may occur on short fades. the backend uses on a . this schedules the ramp in the browser's audio render thread, independent of the animation frame rate. gain transitions are sample-accurate. for production dj-style crossfades: use . for casual "smooth transition" crossfades at 5 s+: either backend works. duration guide | context | recommended duration | | --------------------------------- | -------------------- | | radio / background music | 3–5 s | | dj-style mix | 8–16 s | | album transition | 1–3 s | | "instant" hard cut with preload | 0 s | set duration in : override per-call: lead time: threshold vs duration controls when initiates the crossfade. it must be greater than or equal to : if see also - crossfade api: crossfadeto, istransitioning, crossfadeoptions - autoadvanceplugin: crossfade, crossfadeduration options - backends overview: backend accuracy comparison

title: Equalizer Customization

content: equalizer customization the from inserts a 10-band peaking eq into the web audio graph. this page covers custom presets, band manipulation, and state persistence. prerequisites requires . register first. works with both backends but fully connects the graph to only on . on , it creates a lazily. band frequencies | frequency | notes | | --------- | ---------------------- | | | pre-gain unity = 0 | | 70 hz | sub-bass | | 180 hz | bass | | 320 hz | low-mid | | 600 hz | mid | | 1000 hz | upper-mid | | 3000 hz | presence | | 6000 hz | brilliance | | 12000 hz | air | | 14000 hz | high air | | 16000 hz | ceiling | band gain range: −12 db to +12 db. pre-gain range: −1 to +3 0 = unity gain. preset design guide 19 built-in presets are included access via . to add custom presets, use or supply them in : preset is a partial list, so only the frequencies listed are updated; other bands keep their current gain. this lets a preset target a subset of the chain without resetting the rest. at runtime, add or update a preset without re-registering the plugin: runtime band manipulation listening to eq changes emits for each band mutation and for the full snapshot: persistence persistence is opt-in: set in options and eq state bands, selected preset, pre-gain, custom presets is saved on every change and restored on the next . the default storage backend is . override by passing a custom backend in : pre-gain pre-gain is a global gain stage applied before the filter chain. a value of is unity gain the default. positive values boost, negative values cut. use it to compensate for overall loudness increase when boosting multiple bands: the pre-gain slider range is −1 to +3 wider than band sliders. the underlying receives so maps to unity. see also - audiographplugin, prerequisite for equalizerplugin - backends overview, backend requirements for full graph access - recipes: lyrics and equalizer, combining eq with lyrics in a now playing screen

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common music player issues: no audio, crossfade not firing, lyrics out of sync, backend errors, and diagnostics.
content: troubleshooting no audio plays symptom: resolves, event fires, but no sound. causes and fixes: 1. browser autoplay policy. the browser blocks audio until the user has interacted with the page. call only inside a user gesture click, keydown. 2. volume is 0. check . defaults to 100, but a stored preference may have overridden it. 3. muted. check . call if needed. 4. audio output routed to wrong device. call and verify the target device is listed. use to route to a specific device, or to open the system picker. 5. source url unreachable. open the url directly in the browser. if it 404s or 401s, the track field is wrong or auth is missing. does nothing symptom: call appears to succeed but no audible transition occurs. causes and fixes: 1. selected. the default backend uses a loop for crossfade ~50 fps. it is less accurate than . crossfade is functional but may be imperceptible on short durations. switch with for sample-accurate fades. 2. duration too short. the default is 5 seconds. if your track is shorter than the fade duration, the crossfade completes instantly. reduce in . 3. already transitioning. returns . wait for the event before starting another. 4. fired first. if track end and your manual call overlap, the plugin may have already advanced. use and in options instead of calling manually from . lyrics are not displayed symptom: is registered but no lyrics appear. causes and fixes: 1. no on the track. reads if you set that option, otherwise . if neither is set, no fetch occurs. check your . 2. no custom resolver. without a option on , it uses directly. this still works if the url is correct. 3. unsupported file extension. parser selection is by url extension. and are built-in. custom formats need . 4. cors blocked. the fetch must succeed from the browser. add headers on the lyric host or proxy through your own server. 5. event not fired. listen to . if it never fires, check the network tab for a failed fetch on the lyrics url. lyrics are out of sync symptom: lyrics display at the wrong time. causes and fixes: 1. lrc timestamp format. verify your file uses format. non-standard formats e.g. seconds-only will not parse correctly. 2. seek position not updating lyrics. if the user seeks, re-scans from the cue list. this is automatic. if it is not working, ensure you are listening to not polling . 3. clock drift with . the uses which is sample-accurate but may diverge from after long sessions. this is expected. use not for any sync you build. throws symptom: throws an error. causes and fixes: 1. safari and ios. requires a user gesture on ios. call only inside a click or touch handler. 2. context suspended. the may be suspended after a page visibility change. listen to and call on page show. 3. already using the requested backend. not an error, but verify with before switching. phase stuck in symptom: returns indefinitely. causes and fixes: 1. source url returns a non-media content-type. hls streams must return . mp3/flac must return an audio content-type. a redirect to a login page returns , which hangs the parser. 2. auth token expired and is not set. a 401 with no refresh config produces a stale request. provide in your setup config. 3. hls manifest parse error. enable debug logging to capture the raw error. debug logging enable verbose output: with , the player logs every event, state transition, plugin lifecycle call, and network request to the browser console. filter by to isolate player logs. checking player state programmatically paste this into the browser console at any time to snapshot player state. see also - faq, common questions - configuration, all setup options - events, event reference for logging - backends, capability comparison

title: FAQ
description: Frequently asked questions about the NoMercy Music Player: setup, crossfade, lyrics, backends, and TypeScript.
content: faq can i use this player without the nomercy media server? yes. is a standalone npm package. point it at any reachable audio url, a cdn, an s3 bucket, a local dev server, anything. the server integration , hls stream handling is opt-in. what is the difference between and ? is the concrete class. is the interface you should use for consumer-held references props, context, dependency injection. this prevents consumers from depending on the concrete constructor and keeps the type boundary clean. how many player instances can i have? as many as you need. each call with a unique id creates an independent instance. they share no state and each has its own audio backend, queue, and plugin set. a typical app has one global instance. a multi-room app might have one per room. does the player work server-side ssr/node? not for playback. the player needs browser apis , , , to actually play. construction is ssr-safe — it no-ops the container lookup when is absent and does not throw on import — but transport won't work in node. in ssr frameworks next.js, nuxt, create and drive the player only in browser-side code. why does autoplay block in the browser? browsers require a user gesture before allowing audio playback. common patterns: - call inside a or event handler. - on page load, set up the player and queue, but defer until the first interaction. the event fires when setup is complete. you can queue tracks there, but do not call from unless you know a user gesture has already occurred. what formats are supported? | format | notes | | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | mp3 | universal | | aac / m4a | universal | | flac | all modern browsers | | ogg / opus | chrome, firefox, edge not safari | | wav | universal | | hls | native on safari; handles other browsers | is a production dependency of , which this package depends on, so it arrives transitively. no extra install required for hls. how do i crossfade? two ways: 1. automatic: use with and . the plugin starts the crossfade automatically before each track ends. 2. manual: call from your own code. a manual crossfade always ramps linearly; the option shapes only the automatic autoadvance transition. the default backend uses a loop ~50 fps. for sample-accurate fades, switch to first: what is the difference between and backends? | | | | | --------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------- | | default | yes | no | | crossfade accuracy | ~50 fps raf | sample-accurate | | eq / spectrum plugins | via lazy mediaelementsourcenode | native web audio graph | | ios autoplay | easier | requires user gesture | | memory overhead | lower | slightly higher | switch at any time with . can i switch backends at runtime? yes. disposes the current backend, creates the new one, and re-wires all events. playback pauses during the switch. resume with . how do i persist volume / shuffle / repeat preferences? implement a and pass it in setup: a custom must implement the full interface , , , , — extend or wrap your own backend. the core itself does not persist , , , or — these are held in memory only the config is read by plugins via , not by the core. persist them yourself by listening for the relevant events and writing to your , or let a plugin do it e.g. 's . how do i add lyrics? 1. add to the player. 2. set on each must be a or url. 3. listen to for the active line. see lyrics for full details. can i use a custom lyric format? yes. register a : parser selection is by url extension. the built-in lrc and vtt parsers are registered by default. how do i show a spectrum analyzer or equalizer? both require which routes audio through a web audio graph. it works on either backend: on the default backend it lazily creates a ; gives a full native graph. and are re-exported from the music player's subpath for ergonomic imports: how do i integrate with react? use a custom hook with for the player instance and for reactive state. see react integration for the complete pattern. how do i integrate with vue? use a composable with for reactive state. see vue integration for the complete pattern. is typescript required? no, but strongly recommended. all events, methods, and configuration options are typed. without typescript you lose autocomplete and will have to consult the docs for every method signature. how do i clean up the player? call . this stops playback, removes all event listeners, disposes all plugins, frees the audio backend, and removes the instance from the internal registry. after , calling creates a fresh instance. see also - troubleshooting: error diagnosis - quick start: minimal working example - configuration: all setup options

title: Music Player
description: nomercy-music-player v2, the headless audio engine with sample-accurate crossfade, a dual-backend architecture, and a typed plugin framework.
content: nomercy-music-player is the headless audio engine that powers music on nomercy tv. the tricky part of a music player is the gap between two tracks, and this engine is built around getting it title: What is the Player Core
description: The shared, headless engine the video and music players are built on.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/index.ts / what is the nomercy player core the video player and the music player are mostly the same machine underneath. a queue is a queue, auth is auth, and a plugin system does not care whether it is driving a film or an album. is that shared machine pulled into one package, so the two players do not each carry their own copy. it is headless and you never run it on its own; the library packages bring it along as a dependency. what's in it - transport and a queue engine play, pause, seek, next, shuffle, backlog - the auth pipeline bearer tokens, 401 refresh, 403 propagation - the plugin system and a typed event bus - i18n and storage - an adapter port for every cross-cutting concern, swappable without subclassing the player a fix in any of these lands in both players at once. where it sits the core knows nothing about nomercy server apis or your app; that lives in the layers above it. next steps - quick start: the smallest working setup - architecture: the full five-layer model and how the player is composed - adapter ports: every port and its default - plugins: the built-in plugins shipped with the core

content: versioning three packages, one coordinated version line. current status all three packages are on a pre-release train. install with the tag: do not rely on , as it resolves to the v1 line while the tag is the active development target. version coordination policy the three packages are versioned together. a breaking change to the player core's adapter interfaces requires a major bump across all three packages. the packages always ship at the same version number, such as , , etc. this means: - you can mix with without type mismatches. - mixing different beta numbers is not supported and may produce typescript errors. semver interpretation during beta while the version is , any beta bump may include breaking changes. treat each beta as potentially breaking and read the changelog before upgrading. after the stable release, standard semver applies: - patch : bug fixes only. no api changes. - minor : additive. new methods, new events, new adapter ports. backwards compatible. - major : breaking. full migration guide provided. v1 maintenance the v1 packages , are frozen. no new features. critical security fixes only, on a best-effort basis. migrate to v2 using the per-package migration guides: - video player: v1 to v2 - music player: v1 to v2 - top-level migration overview planned v2.x additions not yet shipped the following plugins are stubbed and throw in v2.0. they are planned for v2.1: | plugin | package | status | | ------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------ | | music | | throws in v2.0 | | music | | throws in v2.0 | | music | | throws in v2.0 | the video player's and are different: they ship and function in v2.0. only the music copies above are v2.1 stubs that throw. kitversion the player core exports a constant matching the package.json version. plugins can use this to assert minimum core versions at registration time via . if the installed core version is below , throws at registration time.

title: Architecture
description: The five-layer model that separates generic player infrastructure from your application code. How the player core, libraries, and plugins relate to each other.
content: architecture the player sdk is organized into five layers so that generic infrastructure never gets tangled up with your application-specific code. each layer only knows about the layer directly below it, and it communicates upward through defined ports. that discipline is what lets you swap a backend, replace a ui plugin, or write a consumer plugin that talks to signalr without any of those changes leaking into the shared core. the five layers no layer may reach "down" past the layer below it or "up" into a layer above it except through a defined port. listed highest to lowest: why this matters the boundary between layer 4 and layer 5 is the enforcement point. anything nomercy-specific lives at layer 5. built-in plugins layer 4 must work for any consumer, with any backend, without any knowledge of the nomercy infrastructure. the practical consequence: when you add a built-in plugin from the package, it does not import from your app. when you write a consumer plugin, it can import from anywhere, but it should not modify core internals. adapter ports layer 2 core exposes a set of named adapter ports. each port has a typed interface and a default implementation. you replace a port only when you need different behavior, for example swapping for , or replacing the browser network monitor with a capacitor native adapter. the video and music library layers add ports of their own on top of these, documented with each library. see core adapters for the full port catalog. plugin layering in practice a typical app setup: layer-5 plugins can listen to events from layer-4 plugins using the typed class-form: three-package layout | npm package | layer | consumers | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | | 2 core + 4 built-in plugins | library authors, advanced consumers writing plugins directly against the core | | | 3 + 4 | anyone building a video player | | | 3 + 4 | anyone building a music player | both library packages re-export everything from the core, so consumers of the video or music player do not need to install the core separately unless they are writing core-level plugins. container class system boundary state classes on the player container element are applied by the core's container-class-emit mixin. they are bare class names with no prefix: , , , , , , , , , , and / for pointer activity. these are core-level, present regardless of which ui plugin is active. the ui overlay controls bar, seek bar, menus, spinner is 's domain. it reads the core's state classes and adds its own dom into the container. never modifies the core state classes; it only reads them. this boundary is intentional: a consumer can build a completely custom ui plugin that responds to the same state classes without touching . the state source core and the ui renderer plugin are decoupled. mixin composition the player prototype is assembled at class definition time from a set of mixins via . each mixin owns one surface: this is why a fix in lands once and applies identically to both the music and video player.

title: Plugins and Adapters
description: The two ways to extend the player, the boundary between them, and when to reach for each.
content: plugins and adapters the player core is small on purpose. it plays a queue, keeps time, and fires events, and that's about it. everything else you build on top of it happens through one of two mechanisms, and almost every "how do i add x" question really comes down to picking the right one of the two. plugins add new behavior a plugin is something the player does that it didn't before: an equalizer, a controls overlay, subtitle rendering, a skip-intro button, casting to a tv. a plugin watches events, reacts to them, and brings its own state and ui along. you opt into each one with , and your bundler drops the ones you never added, so you only ship what you actually use. if you catch yourself wanting the player to do a new thing, you want a plugin. see the plugin system overview for the full picture. adapters swap how something already works an adapter replaces a piece of behavior the player already has with your own version. we call each swappable piece a port. the player always saves settings somewhere, always talks to the network somehow, always reads a clock. each of those is a port with a sensible default already in it. you swap the default when it doesn't fit you, like saving state to your own server instead of the browser. everything else keeps working, because the player only ever talks to the port, never to your implementation directly. if you catch yourself wanting an existing job done differently, you want an adapter. see adapters for every port and how to wire them. when to use which one question sorts almost every case: are you adding something new, or changing something that's already there? - adding something the player didn't do before, that's a plugin. - changing how an existing job gets done, that's an adapter. an equalizer is new behavior, so it's a plugin. saving to your server instead of the browser is the same job done differently, so it's an adapter. and the two team up all the time: a plugin can read from a storage port you swapped, where the plugin brings the behavior and the adapter decides where the data actually lives. for how all of this maps onto the player's layers, from the generic core up to your own app code, read architecture.

title: Auth & Fetch
description: The authFetch wrapper, bearer token injection, 401 vs 403 handling, and retry policy.
content: auth & fetch the player's pipeline handles all network requests made by the player and its built-in plugins. bearer tokens are injected automatically, 401 responses trigger a single refresh attempt, and 403 responses propagate immediately. token storage and security tokens are never stored in or by the core. the player holds the config object in memory only, in the property on the player instance. when you pass a factory function for , the function is called on every authenticated request. the token value is not cached between requests. this means: - page reload clears all tokens, so your app is responsible for restoring auth on mount. - the core never reads from or writes to as part of auth. any interaction is your app's responsibility. - a factory that returns a stale token is the only way to accidentally replay an expired token, so use a factory that always fetches the current token from your auth sdk. configuration all fields are optional. without , requests are unauthenticated. auth config reference token or factory. a factory is called on every authenticated request, use a factory when the token can expire. a static string is applied as-is. the token is injected as . called once when a request returns 401. invoke your auth sdk's refresh logic here. after this resolves, the player re-reads from the config and retries the failed request exactly once with the new value. if refresh fails, fires and the error propagates to the caller. custom request signer, called after the bearer token is applied. use for hmac, api key rotation, or any custom signing scheme. headers appended to every authenticated request. each value can be a static string, a sync getter, or an async getter — same forms as . 401 vs 403 handling | response | behavior | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 401 | called once → request retried. if refresh fails → event + error propagates. | | 403 | error propagates immediately. is never called for 403. | do not lump 401 and 403 together in your error handling. a 403 is an access policy decision, retrying with a refreshed token will not help. check the server's entitlement configuration instead. auth events: retry policy retries failed requests using a built-in per-code policy, — an a map of error-code matcher to . the default is conservative: most codes do not retry, transient ones timeouts, 5xx, fragment loads retry a few times with backoff, and 403 never retries. there is no setup-level retry option. to override retry behaviour for a specific request, pass a as the option on inside a plugin: auth refresh retries are separate from the general retry policy, so is called exactly once, not retried. inside plugins: plugins should use instead of the global . the parameter types the parsed response, no casts needed. the options' | | controls how the body is decoded; pass a custom to transform a body. the player's auth config and retry policy are applied automatically: if you need the raw object before it is dispatched for example, to add a signature, use in the auth config rather than building it manually in the plugin. updating auth at runtime replace auth config after setup, for example, when a long-lived token is refreshed by an external mechanism: this merges the provided partial config with the existing auth config. only the fields you provide are updated.

title: Plugin System Overview
description: What plugins are, the five-layer model, how core plugins differ from library plugins and consumer plugins, and where to find each.
content: plugin system overview the player is split into plugins for everything that most players you find out there just come bundled with, whether you need them or not. the idea is that you can make your player as lean as you want, anywhere from just getting an audio tag to play so you can listen for events and control it, all the way up to the full setup of a streaming platform like nomercy tv. splitting it up this way also lets your bundler strip out all the unused code, so you ship the smallest build you can. it keeps a clean line between the generic stuff and your stuff too. the plugins that ship in the packages know how to do their job and nothing about your app, so they work for anyone. your own plugins are where the app-specific things live, like your server urls or auth, and they can reach for whatever they need. keeping those two apart is most of what keeps things sane as the app grows, and it really comes down to one thing: what a plugin is allowed to import is what decides where it belongs. the architecture page has the full picture, and plugins and adapters covers how a plugin differs from an adapter. what a plugin is a plugin is a class that extends : - : the player type it targets for core-level plugins, or for library-specific plugins - : the options the plugin accepts - : the typed events the plugin emits the base class provides managed resources: , , , , , , . all of these auto-dispose when the plugin is disposed, so no manual cleanup is needed for resources acquired through these methods. layer placement the five-layer model determines where a plugin belongs: | layer | type | rule | | --- | --- | --- | | 4 | built-in plugin | ships in a package. generic behavior: no server urls, no app tokens. works for any consumer. | | 5 | consumer plugin | your app. can import from anywhere. contains nomercy server endpoints, signalr, auth tokens. | both layers use the same base class. the distinction is purely what they import and what goes in their options. plugin scopes plugins live at three different scopes: core plugins shipped inside . these are generic audio, visualization, dom, and coordination plugins that work with any player built on the core. most are in the main barrel export; a few use subpath exports. see built-in core plugins for the full catalogue. library plugins shipped inside the video or music player packages. these are domain-specific to their media type, and each library documents its own. see the video player and music player sections for their plugin pages. consumer plugins written by you. named with a vendor prefix , . these live in your application codebase at layer 5. see plugin authoring for how to write one. registration and lookup for the full registration api see plugin registration. plugin contract every plugin must satisfy the conformance checklist in the plugin standard. the standard is enforced by lint rules in the core. built-in core plugin catalog these plugins ship in . none are registered automatically. | plugin | what it does | import | | --- | --- | --- | | | creates and owns the + signal chain. required by all other audio plugins. | | | | mounts a shared and runs the raf render loop. required by visualization plugins. | | | | chromecast web sender sdk bridge. forwards player state to a cast receiver and mirrors it back. base class, consumers import the video or music player's own subclass. | | | | 10-band parametric eq with pre-gain, named presets, and persistence. requires . | | | | master gain + stereo pan with persistence. requires . | | | | fft analyser. emits events with frequency, waveform, and band-energy data. requires . | | | | abstract base class for canvas visualizations. subclass and override . requires + . | | | | bridge between a host page and a player running inside an . | | | | keyboard binding router. default bindings: space, arrow keys, . configurable scope and cooldown. | | | | wires for os lock-screen controls, hardware media keys, and now playing artwork. | | | | toast notification overlay with transient, persistent, and queued modes. | | | | web locks–based cross-tab election so only one tab plays at a time. | | plugin or adapter? quick rule: adding something new the player does is a plugin; changing how it already does something is an adapter a port swap. they pair up nicely too, like a plugin that reads from a storage port you swapped. plugins and adapters walks through the boundary and when to reach for each. where to go next | goal | page | | --- | --- | | register, look up, or remove a plugin | plugin registration | title: Adapters
description: The core adapter ports. Name, purpose, default implementation, and how to replace each one.
content: core adapter ports we provide the adapter pattern so you can change how the player behaves whenever you have a need that's a bit unique, something that shouldn't be the default for everyone. every piece here, like where state gets saved, how the player talks to a server, or which clock it reads, already has a sensible default wired in. you only reach for an adapter when that default doesn't fit you. say you want the player to remember resume positions and volume on your own server instead of in the browser, so they follow your users from their phone to their tv. you don't fork anything or go digging through player internals for that. you write a small storage adapter that reads and writes against your api, hand it to , and everything else carries on exactly as before. the player never knows where the bytes actually go, it just asks the port and gets an answer. that's really all a port is: a clearly defined slot with a default sitting in it. swapping what's in the slot is how you make the player yours without making it everyone's. this is also the line between an adapter and a plugin. if you're changing how something the player already does works on the inside, that's a port swap. if you're adding something new for the player to do, like an equalizer or a skip button, that's a plugin. plugins and adapters covers when to reach for each. the core ships the ports below. libraries built on the core add ports of their own, documented with whichever library owns them. how to wire a port all ports are wired through : core adapter catalog core infrastructure content: / src: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/storage/ / overview the storage adapter gives plugins a namespaced, async-compatible key-value store. each plugin receives an auto-namespaced wrapper around the shared backend, so plugin keys never collide with each other or with player-level keys. the default backend is . swap it via . istorage interface methods may return values or promises, so synchronous backends and asynchronous ones indexeddb, remote api share one interface. plugin code always uses . built-in backends localstoragebackend default. synchronous. silently falls back to when is blocked third-party cookie restrictions, private browsing mode, ssr. memorystoragebackend in-process memory store. ideal for testing or ssr environments where is absent. data does not persist across page loads. indexeddbbackend asynchronous indexeddb-backed store. use for large values where the 5 mb cap is too small e.g. offline playlist caches, waveform data. plugin storage access inside a plugin, is the auto-namespaced wrapper, so there is no need to prefix keys: the wrapper automatically prefixes all keys with so there is no risk of collision with another plugin's key. custom backend any class implementing works, including an api-backed remote store for cross-device persistence: see also - setup, config field - plugin registration, plugin contract
