content: / src: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/platform/browser.ts / overview the platform adapter bundles every primitive the core hardcodes against browser apis: wake-lock, network monitoring, visibility, codec capabilities, fullscreen, and pip. swapping the bundle lets capacitor, tauri, and electron consumers inject platform-native equivalents in one place. the default ships with the core and works in any modern browser. iplatform interface iwakelock prevents the device display from sleeping while media is playing. throws when the screen wake lock api is absent. call before offering the feature. inetworkmonitor read-only view of the host device's network state. and return on browsers where the network information api is absent firefox, safari as of 2025. the function returns a teardown disposer. ivisibilitymonitor tracks whether the browser tab is currently visible. icapabilitiesprobe queries the runtime for hardware decode capabilities before committing to a stream variant. ifullscreencontroller video only ipipcontroller video only partial override you do not have to replace the entire platform bundle. spread and override only what you need: returns the active platform bundle. available before , returns as the default so early reads don't need a null check. see also - setup: config field, policy - device detection: , - events reference: , , , ,

title: IClock
description: The clock port, IClock interface, the built-in systemClock, and wiring a custom NTP-adjusted or test clock via setup({ clockSource }).
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/clock/iclock.ts / iclock by default the player reads the wall-clock time through . that works fine in most situations. where it falls short is anything that needs to agree on the current moment across multiple devices: group listening sessions, watch parties, or any plugin that schedules actions against a server-side timeline. drifts per device, so two clients that think they're in sync can be off by hundreds of milliseconds. the clock port lets you supply a corrected time source without touching any plugin. you pass a plain function to , and anything that calls picks up your corrected value from that moment on. the interface is the shape you implement when you want a structured object, which you then hand over as . everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter a plain object that wraps . the core uses this value whenever is not configured. you never construct it yourself, but you can import it to use as a fallback inside a custom clock or to verify the contract shape in tests. usage pass any zero-argument function returning a millisecond epoch timestamp: to use a structured implementation, bind its method: after setup, returns whatever your returns. plugins coordinating timestamps should call rather than directly so they transparently pick up any correction you install. interface one method. it returns the current time as a unix-epoch millisecond integer. the simplicity is intentional: anything that can produce a from a moment in time satisfies this contract. custom implementation the common case is a clock corrected by an ntp-style offset you fetch from your own backend: if the sync fails or hasn't run yet, stays 0 and the clock degrades gracefully to . this sync uses the platform on purpose, not the core's built-in , because the round-trip measurement must not be thrown off by automatic retries. that is the exception, not the rule. for ordinary data requests, prefer the built-in client: outside a plugin, or inside one, so your auth and retry policy are applied for you. see auth and fetch. for tests, a controllable fake is the main use case: see also - adapters, the full port catalog - realtime, the websocket channel port, used by group-listening features that pair with a corrected clock

title: Element Factory
description: DOM element creation helpers, createElement, createButton, createSVG, addClasses, removeClasses, and their fluent builder types.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/element-factory/dom.ts / element factory this is not an adapter port in the same sense as the logger or storage. there is no interface to swap and no option. it is a small set of dom utility functions that both player libraries and plugin authors use to create and configure elements without writing verbose chains. the fluent builder pattern means you can create, add classes, set attributes, and insert an element into the dom in one expression rather than four separate statements. all five functions are also available from the subpath: functions creates an element of with the given and returns a fluent builder. when is , an existing element with that is reused instead of creating a second one. this is useful for singleton overlays progress bar, subtitle container that a plugin might try to mount more than once. creates a with and both set to , and the click listener already attached. this is the baseline accessible button pattern the built-in ui plugins use for all controls. creates an element in the svg namespace with , , and set. returns the raw element so you can append , , or children directly. adds css class names to , skipping empty strings. returns a fluent builder so you can chain further operations. removes css class names from , skipping empty strings. returns directly not a builder since removal is typically the last step. builder types the fluent builders are typed so the chain narrows correctly as you go: call at the end of any chain to retrieve the underlying dom element. see also - adapters, the full port catalog

title: IEventBus
description: The event bus port, IEventBus interface, the built-in EventEmitter, and when you would ever swap it.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/event-bus/ieventbus.ts / ieventbus the event bus is the connective tissue between the player, its plugins, and your application code. every , , , and call inside the core goes through , the default implementation. you almost certainly never swap this out. it is wired internally before runs and is not a option. the only realistic reason to replace it is if you are embedding the player inside a reactive store system vuex, pinia, redux and want all events to flow through that store's own event mechanism instead. in that case you implement and hand it to the player constructor directly. built-in adapter a plain emitter. both player classes extend it, so calling is literally calling on the player instance. plugins access it through / , which delegate to the same player-scoped instance. a few design details worth knowing: - registering the same function reference twice for the same event adds it only once, the underlying deduplicates. - stores a wrapper in a keyed on the original handler reference, so can find and remove the wrapper even though the caller never touched it. - snapshots the listener set before iterating, so a handler calling mid-dispatch does not mutate the live iteration. - each listener is wrapped in a try/catch so one bad handler cannot abort the rest of the dispatch chain. - fires a microtask-delayed event when a previously empty event gains its first listener, useful for lazy-load logic. the phantom field on is a compile-time brand used by the generic type inference machinery. it is never assigned at runtime. interface removes every listener across all events. the player calls this during disposal to prevent handler leaks. returns the total live listener count across all events, which the testing leak harness uses to assert that plugins clean up after themselves across use-then-dispose cycles. when you'd replace it you probably won't. this port has no config key because the core constructs the bus before runs. if you do need to replace it, the typical case is routing all player events through an existing pub/sub or store-event system so you can observe them in one place without adding a separate subscriber. implement with the store's publish/subscribe primitives, pass it to the player constructor, and the rest of the core keeps calling without knowing anything changed. see also - adapters, the full port catalog - lifecycle registry, the other internal resource plugins depend on

title: IIdGenerator
description: The ID generator port, IIdGenerator interface, the built-in crypto.randomUUID adapter, and swapping it in tests.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/id-generator/iidgenerator.ts / iidgenerator every plugin instance, every media item, and every internal resource the player creates needs a unique identifier. the core calls to get one, and by default that means . this is almost entirely invisible to you during normal use. the one time you care is in tests: random uuids make snapshot assertions and deterministic test output painful. swapping in a sequential counter makes generated ids predictable and assertion-friendly. there is no key for this adapter. it is a construction-time concern, not a runtime configuration. built-in adapter a plain object that delegates to . in environments where is absent some older workers, non-secure contexts, it falls back to a + suffix, which is collision-resistant enough for non-cryptographic ids. the adapter is a plain object rather than a class because no state is needed: is a pure call with no side effects. interface that is the entire contract. one method, one return value, no configuration. when you'd replace it in production: never. the default is fine and you should not think about it. in tests: swap in a counter so your assertions are not fighting random uuids. the counter resets when you create a new generator instance, so each test suite starts from if you create a fresh one in . see also - adapters, the full port catalog

title: ILifecycleRegistry
description: The lifecycle registry port, ILifecycleRegistry interface, the built-in LifecycleRegistry, and what it tracks for automatic teardown.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/lifecycle-registry/ilifecycleregistry.ts / ilifecycleregistry every plugin gets a lifecycle registry, and it is the main reason plugin authors almost never write manual cleanup code. any listener, timer, observer, fetch signal, or animation frame you register through the registry is automatically cancelled when the plugin is disposed. you never construct one yourself. the player core creates a fresh for each plugin instance and hands it to the plugin as . you call its methods to register resources, and handles the rest in a single call when the player or plugin tears down. there is no key for this adapter. it is an internal construction detail, not a configurable option. built-in adapter tracks six categories of disposable resource: dom event listeners, timers, intervals, disconnect-able observers , , etc., instances, and loops. tears them all down in order: listeners first, then timers and intervals, then raf loops, then observers, then abort controllers, and finally user-registered cleanup callbacks in reverse registration order most-recently-registered runs first, like a stack unwind. is idempotent: calling it twice is safe, the second call is a no-op. if is called after , the callback runs immediately rather than being queued. interface a few things worth noting: - returns the observer unchanged so you can chain: . - is a no-op in ssr environments where is absent. - and return after disposal rather than a live timer id. - exceptions thrown inside timeout, interval, frame, and cleanup callbacks are caught and logged so one bad callback does not abort the teardown sequence. when you'd replace it almost never. the built-in implementation covers everything plugin authors need and its behaviour is well-defined. the one hypothetical: if you are running the player in a custom environment where the web apis , , are shimmed or unavailable, you might need a registry that delegates to those shims. in that case, implement with your environment's equivalents. see also - adapters, the full port catalog - event bus, the other core internal both players and plugins share

title: ILogger
description: The logging port, ILogger interface, the built-in Logger, adding a sink, and wiring a custom logger like Pino or Sentry.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/logger/ilogger.ts / ilogger by default the player and all its plugins log through a small console logger. how noisy it gets is gated by the you set at , which is fine while you're building. in production you usually want those lines going somewhere you can actually see them, like sentry breadcrumbs or your own telemetry. you also don't want every plugin to know about it. the logger port is how you do that from one place. most of the time you don't even replace it: you add a sink to the built-in logger and let your console logs flow to a second destination too. when you'd rather route everything through a logging library you already use, you wrap that library in the shape and hand it to . either way, the core and every plugin keep calling and never notice the difference. everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter a console logger that supports multiple sinks. the core creates one root instance per player, and every plugin shares it through a scoped . you only construct one yourself when you want to pre-register a sink before handing it to . log levels levels run from quiet to loud: , , , , , . each line emits only when the active threshold is at or above its level. the default is , and you set it with at setup rather than touching the logger directly: adding a sink this is the common case, and it doesn't replace anything. build the default , attach a sink, and pass it in. your normal console output keeps working; the sink just gets a copy. interface plugin authors never construct a logger. they receive already scoped to their plugin id, so anything they log shows up tagged with where it came from. custom implementation when you'd rather route everything through a logging library you already run, wrap it in : if your logging library has no multi-sink concept, keeping one destination and no-opping is fine. just document it, like the comment above does. see also - metrics and diagnostics, what the player logs and measures - adapters, the full port catalog

title: IMediaList
description: The media list port, IMediaList interface, the built-in MediaList, cursor semantics, and the full mutation and event API.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/media-list/imedialist.ts / imedialist both and use a single instance as their queue. rather than maintaining parallel list state in each library, all queue methods delegate here: append, remove, shuffle, sort, and everything else. the list is cursor-aware, meaning it always knows which item is current and keeps the cursor stable as items are added, removed, or reordered around it. you almost never replace this. there is no key for it. replacing it would only make sense if you needed the queue to be backed by an external data source a server-side playlist api, an indexeddb store rather than kept in memory. built-in adapter an in-memory, cursor-aware list that extends . must extend , which requires at minimum an field. cursor semantics: - is when items exist and when the list is empty. - every mutation that shifts item positions also shifts the cursor to keep it pointing at the same item. removing the item before the current decrements the cursor by one. removing the current item clamps the cursor to the new last index. - accepts the item itself, its , a zero-based index, or a predicate function, first match wins. every mutation method fires a specific event followed by a event. subscribe to when you only care that something changed. subscribe to the narrower events , , , etc. when you need to know what changed. interface events emits these events. fires after every other mutation event. | event | payload | |-------|---------| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | a few method notes: - preserves the cursor by item when possible. if the previously current item is still in the new list, the cursor moves to its new index. if not, the cursor resets to . - replaces an item by in place, no cursor change, no events. callers that need to notify listeners must do so themselves. - does nothing if or either index is out of range. - uses fisher-yates and the cursor follows the current item to its new position. - also follows the current item after reordering. - clears all items, resets the cursor to , and removes all event listeners. when you'd replace it the in-memory default is sufficient for most players. if you need the queue to reflect a server-side playlist that can be updated externally e.g. a shared watch party queue, you would implement backed by that remote state and emit the same events when it changes. notice this calls rather than the platform . is the player core's built-in client, so your bearer token, retry policy, and events all come along for free. inside a plugin you reach the exact same client through . reach for the built-in one by default and only drop to the platform when you have a reason to. see auth and fetch. see also - in the same app, and spinning up bare websockets next to them creates two competing connection stacks. when that happens, you swap the transport by passing a factory to . every plugin that opens a channel then gets your transport instead, and nothing else changes. you can also override the transport for a single connection by passing in the per-call options, without touching the global default. everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter a that wraps the browser's native to satisfy . the core uses it as the final fallback when no is configured. it normalises the four dom events , , , into the channel's / listener model, maps from numeric constants to the string literals the interface defines, and shields listeners from each other so an error in one handler doesn't stop the rest from firing. reconnection is not built into the adapter itself. the lifecycle layer above it handles reconnect and disposal so every transport, including custom ones, title: IUrlResolver
description: The URL resolver port, IUrlResolver interface, ResolvedUrl, UrlCategory, and wiring a custom CDN signing or per-category routing resolver.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/url-resolver/iurlresolver.ts / iurlresolver every url the player touches, whether a media manifest, a subtitle file, a poster image, or a drm license endpoint, passes through the url resolver before it reaches a element, a worker, or a cast receiver. the built-in resolver applies your token-injection callback and then parses the result into a structured you can inspect. that covers most cases. where you need more is when different asset types need different treatment. a cdn might require per-request signed urls on media and subtitles, but let poster images through unsigned. a multi-origin setup might route files to one edge and font assets to another. the port handles all of that from one place, and the rest of the core never knows the difference. you supply a resolver at or swap it at runtime with . when you only need to extend the built-in behavior rather than replace it, call inside your resolver and let the default path handle any category you don't want to intercept. everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter there is no exported class for the default resolver. when no is configured, the player applies to the raw url string and parses the result into a internally. if you only need to add an auth token to every request, is the right place for it and you do not need to supply a at all. url categories the player core passes a category string alongside every url so your resolver can branch on asset type. the built-in category constants are: custom plugins may pass any string. your resolver should treat unknown categories as a passthrough rather than an error. the resolvedurl shape your resolver returns a object. the player hands this directly to the appropriate consumer, so is what ends up in or the cast receiver. use to gate on file type. it strips query strings for you, so gives , not . the urlresolvercontext shape the second argument to your resolver function carries everything you need to make a routing decision: call to delegate back to the built-in pipeline for any category you don't want to handle yourself. interface a resolver is a callable interface, not a class. the simplest valid implementation is a plain function. custom implementation the common case is signing media and subtitle urls with a short-lived cdn token while leaving everything else to the default pipeline: the token fetch uses , the core's built-in client, so it carries your auth and retry policy automatically. inside a plugin the same client is , and you should prefer it over the platform by default. see auth and fetch. you can also swap the resolver after setup, for example when the user switches between a public and authenticated session: for multi-origin routing, where different asset types come from different hosts: see also - logger, the logging port - adapters, the full port catalog

title: ABR and Bandwidth
description: bandwidth(), bandwidthEstimator(), canPlay(), and CanPlayResult: throughput estimation and device capability probing.
content: abr and bandwidth three methods that expose throughput estimation and decode-capability probing. bandwidth last-known throughput estimate in bits per second. returns until an active stream source reports a measurement the player core itself does not drive estimation, the value comes from the active backend or a consumer-supplied estimator. the value is updated by the active stream source whenever it completes a segment download. on networks where the backend does not report throughput native or without hls, remains . bandwidthestimator read or replace the bandwidth estimator function. reading returns the currently wired estimator or if none is set. writing installs a custom estimator. the active stream source calls the function on every abr level decision. install your own estimator when you have out-of-band signal signalr quality report, server-sent bitrate hint that is more accurate than the default download-speed measurement. the estimator is called synchronously on the abr decision path, so keep it fast. canplay probes whether the browser can decode a specific media profile smoothly. delegates to the platform adapter's bridge, which wraps the standard api. canplayresult means the codec is not supported, so do not select this quality level. means the level is playable but the browser may drop frames under load, so use it as a last resort only. is typically seen on mobile devices with high-bitrate streams that the cpu decodes in software rather than through the hardware decoder pipeline. it is informational, and takes precedence for quality selection. using canplay for quality filtering before rendering a quality picker, filter out levels the browser cannot handle: for hls streams, the video player's hdr-aware abr logic does this filtering automatically, using internally to exclude hdr levels on sdr displays. calling manually is only needed when building a custom quality ui that must pre-filter the level list. see also - media tracks: and - player state: for the abr/manual mode flag - metrics: in - platform: the platform port

title: Plugin Authoring
description: How to write a plugin for the NoMercy Player SDK. Lifecycle, events, error handling, advisories, and the conformance checklist.
content: plugin authoring plugins are the extension point for the player sdk. every feature beyond core transport lives in a plugin: the built-in ui, eq, lyrics, skip markers, chromecast handoff. your app-specific features follow the same contract. for the locked conformance document that lint rules enforce, see plugin standard. before you write a plugin decide which layer your plugin belongs to: - layer 4 built-in: generic domain behavior. no nomercy server urls, no signalr, no app tokens. should work for any consumer. - layer 5 consumer: your app-specific glue. can import from anywhere. both layers use the same base class. the distinction is what they import and what goes in their options. typing your plugin's player generic the generic controls which player api your plugin can access. - use for core-level plugins that don't touch the active item analytics, error reporters, adapters. , , and all transport methods are available directly. - add when your plugin needs . both and satisfy this constraint structurally. - use the concrete player type , when you need library-specific methods like or . plugins that don't read the active item omit ; , , and transport methods are on directly. minimal plugin skeleton usage: identity fields every plugin must declare three static fields: the is the globally unique key. core-shipped plugins use bare kebab-case , . third-party plugins must use a vendor prefix , . lifecycle is called during . return a if you need to load config or register async resources, so fires only after all plugins' promises resolve. is called on or . all timers, intervals, animation frames, and dom mounts registered through the plugin's helper methods , , , auto-dispose, so you only need to explicitly clean up external resources. lifecycle helpers allocate every resource through one of these protected helpers instead of the raw browser api. each one registers its own teardown with the plugin's lifecycle registry, so it is released automatically on and you never write the cleanup yourself. is reserved for the things the kit cannot see — third-party library instances, custom observers, a . | helper | returns | replaces | released on dispose | | ------ | ------- | -------- | ------------------- | | | | | listener removed | | | handle | | timer cleared | | | handle | | timer cleared | | | cancel | a loop | loop cancelled | | | | | called | | | | | channel closed | | | | | node removed | | | | a in | stays once per id | listeners and timers is the one to reach for over a raw — an untracked listener is the most common source of ghost handlers firing after the player is gone. and return their numeric handle if you want to clear one early; most callers discard it. animation frames, and cancelling one yourself drives a loop and hands your callback the frame delta and the timestamp. the loop is cancelled automatically on — but it also returns a disposer so you can stop one loop early, by hand, without tearing down the whole plugin: that is the answer to "how do i dispose a loop programmatically": keep the returned function and call it. for a single deferred write rather than a continuous loop, use instead. abort controllers, sockets, mounts, and styles auth-aware http and auth-aware url resolution are covered under auth and fetch; under internationalisation. event listening always use inside a plugin, never . the form auto-disposes with the plugin. , , and have the same overloaded shapes. emitting events error handling never throw raw errors or call directly. use aborts the current flow, returns or surfaces without aborting. both carry a that decides what the error means: | severity | channel | aborts flow? | meaning | | -------- | ------- | ------------ | ------- | | | | yes | unrecoverable. the player is going down. consumer tears down or shows a fatal screen. | | | + | yes | recoverable. this operation failed, but the plugin keeps running for future events. | | | + | no | degradation. playback continues, consumer is informed. | | | | no | observability only. | does not auto-dispose the player, it raises the contract-level "shutting down" signal. the consumer decides the teardown: disabling a plugin in response to an error is a separate concern, so declare it as a recovery action, not a severity. static error recovery declare a recovery policy to control what happens when a specific error code is emitted by the player or by a dependency: options: | | | . these are declared per plugin through ; there is no setup-level override. plugin dependencies declare required or optional plugin dependencies using class references, never string ids: phase advisories declare which phases are safe for each method. when a guarded mutation matches, the player emits the advisory's severity event / / — in all environments, not just development: plugin replacement and extension replace a built-in plugin with the same id: extend without replacing: dom and storage testing provides a fresh player with the plugin registered, auto-disposes in , and automatically asserts no listener leak after each test. conformance checklist before shipping a plugin: - is vendored - is a valid semver string - is a one-liner - and are defined or inherited - all listeners use never - all timers use / / - all errors use / - every mutator has a paired reader - plugin's generic is declared and exported - is declared when depending on other plugins - tests cover behavior and

title: Recipes
description: Cookbook-style guides for common player setups beyond hello-world. Pick the recipe that matches your feature.
content: recipes the player core handles concerns that every player shares: auth, storage, session persistence, and system integration. these recipes show you how to wire those concerns up in real projects, whether you are building on the video player, the music player, or your own player on top of . each guide is self-contained with working code you can drop straight in. prerequisites: a working install from the core quickstart. core recipes | recipe | what it solves | | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | media session | system mediasession integration, lock-screen metadata, artwork | | persistence | storage adapter selection, saving playback position, restoring on reload | | auth and tokens | authfetch wrapper, refresh-on-401, propagating-on-403 | library-specific recipes anything tied to a media type lives with that library, not here. subtitles, chapters, quality selection and keyboard shortcuts are video concerns; crossfade, gapless and lyrics/eq are music concerns. - video player recipes: subtitles, chapters, quality selection, playlist/queue, keyboard shortcuts, live transcoding - music player recipes: playlist/queue, crossfade and gapless, lyrics and equalizer what to read next - advanced: production patterns: custom adapters, custom backends, ssr, multi-instance, performance - plugin authoring: build your own plugin - core adapters: swap any of the 28 infrastructure ports

title: Media Session
description: System MediaSession integration via MediaSessionPlugin: lock-screen controls, notification metadata, and album artwork.
content: media session lock-screen controls, browser media notification widgets, and hardware media key support. both the video and music players support this via . the media session api is a browser standard that exposes playback controls to the os: android lock screen, ios control center, windows system tray, desktop browser toolbars, and hardware media keys keyboards, headsets, remotes. basic setup that is all that is needed. the plugin reads , , , and artwork / / / from the current queue item and writes them to the music library maps its field to at the library layer. it wires , , , , , , , and action handlers. video player the setup is identical for the video player: for video, the plugin reads and from the item. multiple artwork sizes browsers prefer the largest artwork that fits the display. provide multiple sizes for the best result: when is a string single url, the plugin wraps it in a single-entry array with . customizing metadata override how the plugin builds by subclassing: observing media key actions if you need to respond to media key presses independently e.g. for analytics: browser support the media session api is available in chrome 73+, firefox 82+, safari 15+, and edge 79+. on unsupported browsers, detects the absence of at time and self-disables gracefully, no errors thrown. what to read next - recipes: keyboard shortcuts, pairing media key handling with custom keyboard bindings - recipes: persistence, saving playback position so resuming from lock screen continues from the right point - music: api methods, , , field reference

title: Persistence
description: Choosing a storage backend, saving playback position, and restoring it on the next page load.
content: persistence saving and restoring playback state across page loads: resume position, last-played track, volume level, subtitle preferences. the player core's storage adapter system handles all of this. prerequisites: core: adapters covers the three built-in storage backends. storage backends three implementations ship with the core: built-in plugins write to storage under a per-plugin namespace . the player core itself reads and writes nothing — is consumed only by plugins, via . what persists the core persists nothing on its own. volume, mute, and language live in memory for the session unless you persist them — listen for the relevant events and write to yourself, or let a plugin do it: - persists eq state when you set its option. - persists subtitle style preferences. playback position is likewise not saved automatically, because the core does not know where your server stores watch history. that requires a consumer plugin. saving and restoring playback position write a consumer plugin that saves position to your backend. is typed against directly because it calls — satisfies structurally. for a portable alternative typed against the interface, use . register it: local-only position saving no server for a purely client-side implementation, use directly: reads from the same backend the player is configured with. keys are automatically namespaced. choosing the right storage backend for your context | scenario | backend | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | standard web app | default | | ssr next.js, nuxt | on server, on client. see advanced: ssr | | test suite | , no cross-test contamination | | large eq preset library | | | sync across devices | custom backend calling your api | indexeddb backend for large data eq snapshots, subtitle caches: is async internally. the interface allows async returns etc. so the built-in satisfies it natively. writes complete asynchronously; reads return the last committed value. for a fully async custom backend, see advanced: custom adapter. what to read next - core: adapters: full interface and the backend catalog - advanced: custom adapter: writing an async indexeddb-worker backend - recipes: lyrics and equalizer: eq state is persisted through this same storage system

title: Auth and Tokens
description: Wiring the authFetch wrapper, handling refresh-on-401, ensuring 403 propagates, and writing a custom auth adapter.
content: auth and tokens when your media sources require authorization: hls streams behind a cdn auth wall, apis that return 401 when tokens expire, or endpoints that enforce access control via 403. prerequisites: the auth config is the same on video and music players. for the full reference see core: auth and fetch. minimal auth setup the player injects on every hls manifest and segment request. 401 vs 403: a hard rule | status | what happens | | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 401 | called once → re-read → request retried → if refresh fails, the request rejects with on the channel | | 403 | error propagates immediately. is never called. | do not lump 401 and 403 in the same catch block. a 403 is an entitlement decision, so retrying with a refreshed token achieves nothing. the right response to a 403 is to check the user's subscription or permissions on your server. static vs factory token use the factory form whenever the token can expire. a stale static string will cause 401s until the page is refreshed. updating auth at runtime after , replace the auth config without recreating the player: useful when a user signs in during a session or when a long-lived token is refreshed by an external mechanism. static extra headers add headers to every authenticated request e.g. app version, device id: custom request signing hmac, signed urls for non-bearer auth schemes, use : is called after is applied. both can be used together. using authfetch inside plugins inside a plugin, always use instead of the global . this applies the player's auth config, respects the retry policy, and integrates with error reporting: retry policy by default only specific error codes retry : 5xx and timeouts a few times with backoff, fragment loads up to 5; generic 4xx and unmatched failures use no retry. auth refresh is separate — is called exactly once, never retried. there is no setup-level retry option. to override retry behaviour for a specific request, pass a as the option on inside a plugin: what to read next - core: auth and fetch: full interface reference - advanced: custom adapter: writing a fully custom auth adapter for non-standard signing schemes - recipes: persistence: auth tokens + watch position working together

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common setup and runtime problems with the NoMercy Player SDK. Symptoms, causes, and fixes, verified against core source.
content: troubleshooting every entry below is verified against the core source. if the symptom you're hitting isn't here, file an issue with a minimal reproduction. octopus ass/ssa subtitles do not render symptom: ass/ssa subtitles are enabled and selected, but nothing appears on screen. no errors in the console. cause: uses a dynamic and falls back to a degraded no-render mode if the package isn't present. the plugin never throws, it stays silent. fix: is a regular dependency of , so it should already be present after . if your bundler tree-shakes it out or you are using a selective install, add it explicitly: confirm the degraded mode is the cause: set and look for log lines. a degraded-mode line confirms the dynamic import failed; any other error message tells you something else is wrong. player never reaches symptom: hangs indefinitely. the event never fires. causes and fixes: 1. a plugin's returned a promise that never resolves. awaits all promises capped by , default 30 seconds before emitting . audit each registered plugin for async work without timeouts. 2. the container element doesn't exist in the dom at . the core doesn't wait for the element to appear. ensure returns a non-null element before calling . 3. a plugin's rejected. check the console for events. the failed plugin is disabled; still fires for the remaining plugins. if you see no and no , the promise is stuck see 1. 4. you're inspecting the wrong instance. returns the same instance on every call with the same id. if two parts of your code call setup on different ids, they're different players. dev mode: hls manifest fails to load symptom: locally served files fail when opening the html directly via . cause: browser security policy blocks cross-origin requests from origins. hls segment fetches from any other origin including are blocked. fix: serve over : or use vite / webpack dev server / any local http server. framework ssr: player crashes during server-side render symptom: build or render crashes with or during ssr next.js, nuxt, sveltekit, astro. cause: the player depends on browser apis , , , . these don't exist in a node server environment. fix: lazy-load the player on the client only. next.js react: nuxt / vue: astro: use so the component never renders on the server. pick the directive that matches the component's framework: sveltekit: guard with from , or use which only fires client-side. two players on the same page share state symptom: two players appear to share state, controlling one affects the other. cause: and are factories backed by an internal registry. calls with the same return the same instance. two components using the same id are pointing at the same player. fix: use unique ids per instance: for a single-player app, picking a static id is fine. for multi-player uis pip, watch parties, tile grids, generate a stable id per slot. volume resets every page load symptom: the player ignores the user's saved volume preference. cause: the core doesn't auto-persist volume, that's a plugin concern. fix: persist it in a small plugin via the namespaced storage adapter , not raw . volume is on the 0–100 scale. thrown by music player method symptom: calling on a music player throws with code . cause: audio backends don't have subtitle tracks. is on the shared player surface but is intentionally not implemented on . fix: catch the error by type. import from the core: or, simpler, only call on video players. , , or throws on symptom: adding these music-player plugins, then fires with a . still fires for the remaining plugins. cause: all three are stubbed in and intentionally throw . full implementations are planned for . fix: don't register them yet. track progress in versioning. hls auth: segments return 401 after a delay symptom: hls manifest loads, playback starts, then segment requests start returning 401 after some time. or every segment 401s from the first request. cause token expiry: is a static string. the core injects whatever value you passed at setup. if the token expires between manifest load and segment fetch, the injected value is stale. cause no refresh: isn't configured. the core retries a 401 exactly once if a refresh function is provided; without it, the request fails immediately. fix: pass as a factory and provide a refresh function: the factory is called on every authenticated request, so the player always sees the current token. on a 401, is called once and the request retries automatically. a 403 propagates and is never retried. that's an access-policy problem on the server, not an auth-token problem. inline of the core fails: symptom: a consumer or a custom plugin imports from and the resolver can't find it. cause: the core is the foundation under both and but isn't a transitive runtime dependency a consumer would see. if you're writing a plugin or adapter against the core directly, you need to install the core alongside. fix: if you only use the video or music package's surface no custom plugins, you don't need this, the per-library package re-exports what you need. container element class never updates symptom: the container should gain the bare state classes / alongside the base class but they are missing. cause: state classes live on the element passed as to . if you re-mount the player into a fresh dom node e.g. ssr hydration replacing the host element, the core's reference is to the old node. fix: don't re-create the container after setup. if you have to hmr, spa navigation, the player first and again on the new node. state classes are owned by the core itself, not by , so you get them even on a raw html container with no ui plugin installed. custom plugin's never fires symptom: a plugin declares with recovery actions but nothing happens when it throws. cause: is a declarative map of error code to a recovery action: . the core consults it when the plugin throws via . if your plugin throws directly with or emits via , the recovery map is bypassed. fix: always raise plugin errors through the base class helper: see plugin standard §1.8 for the full error escalation contract. plugin runs twice / plugin event listeners double up symptom: event handlers in a plugin's fire twice for every event. cause: most commonly, is being called manually in addition to the player calling it. don't invoke yourself, triggers the lifecycle. second cause: two different classes share the same . the kit allows this for replacement subclass with same id replaces the original but if both are added independently, both register and both listen. fix: ensure each plugin id is unique. use ids for third-party plugins , to avoid collisions with core-shipped plugins. reporting a bug if the symptom isn't here, file an issue with: - core version from - player package + version - browser + version - minimal html/js reproduction a public codesandbox / stackblitz link is ideal - console output with enabled

content: / src: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/core/mixins/experimental.ts, types/experimental.ts / overview the namespace is a tier-4 override surface for behaviour changes not covered by events, , or subclass hooks. it lets consumers and plugins monkey-patch player methods at runtime without touching the prototype. use this as a last resort. before reaching for , check whether a event listener or a plugin advisory solves the problem. temporarily replace a player method with a custom implementation. the original method is captured on first call. multiple overrides of the same method overwrite each other, the last writer wins. returns a zero-arg disposer; call it to undo the override. | parameter | type | description | | --------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | | | name of the method to override | | | | replacement function called with the player as | returns: , call to restore the original remove the active override for and restore the original implementation. no-op when the method has no active override. snapshot of all active overrides. is always — is a consumer-only api plugin code is lint-blocked from calling it, so it records regardless of caller. returns: plugin lint rule the eslint rule flags any call to from inside plugin code. plugin authors must add an eslint disable comment with a written reason: consumer app code is free to use it without lint friction. restoring an override returns a function — call it to undo that one override. there is no automatic restore: overrides persist until you call the returned function, and does not touch them. see also - events reference, , , and other cancellable events prefer these over - mutation guards, advisory system

title: Custom Adapter
description: Full walkthrough writing a custom IStorage backend backed by IndexedDB Workers, and a custom ITranslator from a CMS. Includes lifecycle hooks, error handling, and the testing pattern.
content: custom adapter when the default adapter implementations don't fit: async persistence indexeddb workers, translations from a cms, or any other infrastructure replacement. prerequisites: core: adapters for the port catalog. core: testing for the test harness. what an adapter is an adapter is a class that implements a typed interface from the core. you wire it through and the player and its plugins use your implementation instead of the default. there are 28 core-level ports plus 4 video-specific and 6 music-specific ones. this guide walks through two of the most commonly replaced ones: 1. : persistence backend synchronous interface, but you can build async internally 2. : translation backend load strings from a cms or i18n service istorage: custom persistence backend the interface title: Custom Plugin
description: Production-grade plugin development: state management, event listening, multi-instance safety, dispose contract, advisories, and a watch-party-lite worked example.
content: custom plugin building a production plugin: one that ships to users, runs in multiple player instances, or coordinates across components. the plugin authoring page covers the basics. this page covers the hard parts. the dispose contract every resource you acquire in must be released in , or through a managed helper. the player core provides helpers that auto-dispose so you don't have to track them manually: | resource | managed helper | manual alternative | | ------------------ | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | event listeners | | in | | timers | | in | | intervals | | in | | animation frames | | in | | dom nodes | | in | | external resources | none, you must clean up manually | websocket, worker, etc. | if you create a or inside a plugin, close/terminate it in : state management keep plugin state private and expose only what consumers need: multi-instance safety when multiple player instances exist on the same page, each plugin instance is isolated: , , , and are all scoped to their own player. there is no shared mutable state between instances unless you introduce it. be careful with singletons: if you need cross-instance coordination for example, pausing all others when one starts, use the realtime channel adapter or a shared event bus: phase advisories advisories let the player core flag a method called at the wrong lifecycle phase: when a guarded mutation matches, the player emits the advisory's severity event / / on the player — in all environments. it is an event, not a console-only warning, and it is not gated on . static onerror recovery declare what happens when specific error codes are emitted by the player or a dependency: options: | | | . worked example: watch-party-lite plugin a plugin that syncs play/pause and seek position across browser tabs using : usage: testing a complex plugin what to read next - plugin authoring, the complete plugin contract reference - plugin standard, the locked conformance rules - advanced: multi-instance, coordinating multiple player instances at the page level - core testing, full test harness reference

title: Writing a Backend
description: Registering a custom IStreamFactory to handle new protocols or MSE pipelines alongside the built-in HLS and native backends.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/stream/istreamsource.ts / writing a backend supporting a streaming protocol or media pipeline the built-in backends don't cover: mpeg-dash, smooth streaming, or a custom mse pipeline. the extension point is and from . prerequisites: streams covers the default hls and native stream factories. read it first, because many needs can be addressed by configuring hls.js rather than writing a new factory. when to write a custom stream factory before writing a factory, check whether the need can be addressed with lower-effort options: 1. hls.js config override: tune bitrate caps, retry counts, or level limits through the setup option. 2. stream interceptor: intercept manifest and segment responses before hls.js sees them via . useful for signing urls or transforming responses. 3. custom plugin: if the need is behavioral custom abr, buffer management, write a plugin that calls existing player methods rather than owning the media pipeline. replace the factory only when none of the above covers the use case. registering a custom factory adds the factory to the . when a url is resolved, each registered factory's is called in registration order. the first factory that returns wins. the built-in hls and native factories are always present as fallbacks. the istreamfactory interface is called for every url the player resolves. return only when your factory can handle it. use the optional argument to decline when the device cannot decode the stream. is called at most once per url resolution and must return an . the istreamsource interface is one of . the events a source can emit are: | event | payload | when | | ----- | ------- | ---- | | | | playlist / header parsed; levels are available | | | | abr or manual call changed the active quality | | | | abr evaluated but did not switch | | | | a media segment finished downloading | | | | an encrypted segment was encountered | | | | a fatal or non-fatal error occurred | minimal shaka player factory dash register it on the player: from this point, any url in the playlist resolves through shaka instead of hls.js or the native element. what to read next - streams: the full / reference and the built-in hls and native factories - adapter ports: every swappable port the core exposes - advanced: custom plugin: adding behavior on top of any backend

title: Multi-Instance
description: Running multiple players on one page: PiP + main player, watch-party tile grid, tab-leader pattern, and event-bus isolation between instances.
content: multi-instance running more than one player on the same page: a mini-player or pip alongside a main player, a grid of synchronized tiles, or a podcast player in the background while a video plays. how instances are isolated each call to or returns a scoped player singleton keyed by . two players with different ids are completely independent: - separate event buses - separate plugin registries - separate queue state there is no shared mutable global between two player instances unless you introduce it explicitly e.g. a or a shared module-level variable. two players on one page pip + main player pattern the browser's native picture-in-picture api keeps one element in a floating window. the player exposes pip control: no second player instance is needed for native pip, the single player's element moves to the pip window. watch-party tile grid for a grid of synchronized tiles each playing the same content: tab-leader pattern when multiple browser tabs have the same player open e.g. a podcast player that persists across navigation, elect a leader tab that owns playback. other tabs follow. use for cross-tab communication: in practice, use the watchpartyliteplugin worked example as a starting point and extend it with a leader election algorithm. event-bus isolation two player instances never share an event bus. if you need a player to react to another player's events, wire them explicitly: for more complex cross-instance protocols, write a coordinator object outside both players: storage namespacing storage is namespaced by plugin id, not player id: a plugin's keys are prefixed the player core writes nothing itself. so two player instances that share one storage backend and register the same plugin will share those keys. to isolate per player, give each instance its own storage backend, or derive per-instance plugin ids. if you want two players to share a storage state e.g. the same volume preference, pass the same backend instance through and use a shared key namespace: what to read next - title: Testing
description: Using the testing subpath stub player for plugin unit tests. describePlugin, assertNoListenerLeak, and the stub backend.
content: testing the player core ships a subpath with utilities for writing unit tests against plugins without a real browser. install the testing utilities are included with the core package. no additional install is needed: import from the testing subpath: wraps a test suite with a fresh player and registered plugin per test. auto-disposes in . arguments: verifies that a plugin's cleans up all event listeners. this is a required test for all plugins. snapshots the listener count before and after a setup/teardown cycle. if the count after teardown exceeds the count before setup, the test fails with details of the leak. already runs a leak assertion automatically after each test. use directly only when you need to test a non-plugin subject or run cycles across multiple setup/teardown pairs via . stub player the stub player is a minimal implementation with no browser dependencies. it: - supports the full event bus , , , - supports , , , , , and all transport stubs - does not start actual media playback - works in node.js without a dom vitest, jest you can use the stub player directly for lower-level testing: mock fetch returns a self-contained fetch stub. assign to the plugin's property to intercept outgoing requests: integration with vitest the core's test suite uses vitest. if you are using a different runner jest, the testing utilities still work, as the subpath has no vitest imports. for plugins that mount dom elements use , use or as the test environment.

title: FAQ
description: Frequently asked questions about the NoMercy Player SDK.
content: faq do i need to install the core if i'm just using the video player? no. and both re-export everything from . install only the package you need. the core is a separate install only if you are writing plugins that work against the raw core interface without a library package. can i use both the video player and music player on the same page? yes. each player instance is isolated by its id. the video player and music player share no global state beyond the internal instance registry. they do not interfere. you can have both playing at the same time subject to browser audio policy. if you need one to pause when the other plays, wire that coordination yourself in a consumer plugin or in your app code. how do i write my own subtitle renderer? replace the built-in vtt text rendering with your own plugin that implements the same interface. register your plugin with . for ass/ssa subtitles with full typesetting, add , which loads dynamically and handles its own rendering. do not combine and a custom renderer for the same subtitle track. see video, subtitle overlay for the full api. does the player handle 401 / 403 differently? yes. the auth pipeline treats them differently by design: - 401, token expired. is called once, the new token is applied, and the request is retried. if refresh fails, the request errors with the event itself fires from . - 403, access denied. the error propagates immediately. is never called for 403s. the server has denied access even with valid credentials. never lump 401 and 403 in the same catch block. a 403 may signal an entitlement problem that no amount of token refreshing will fix. how do i add auto-advance play next track when the current one ends? on the video player it is built in and on by default — set in to turn it off. on the music player, add : the music plugin listens to the event and calls . when crossfade is enabled, it triggers instead. how do i pause all players at once? there is no global play/pause. you control each instance by id: if you need coordinated playback across multiple players group listening, use , planned for v2.1. can i use the player with typescript strict mode? yes. the packages ship full typescript types. all public methods are typed. the generic parameter or threads your playlist item type through , , , and events, no casts required. how do i render the player without the built-in ui? do not add . the player itself renders nothing, all chrome is opt-in through plugins. build your own controls using the event api: how do i restrict hls quality to avoid high bitrate on slow networks? is not related to quality. quality selection lives in the video player's hls adapter. set a maximum level via the config: to hard-cap to a specific quality level index at runtime: hdr-aware abr is automatic, so on sdr displays, the player filters out hdr levels from the abr selection pool. no configuration needed. see video, hls for the full quality api. how do i listen to events from a plugin i did not write? use the string form with the auto-namespaced event name on : plugin events are always namespaced as . the class-form is only available inside a subclass body, it is a method and does not exist on the external surface. is the player compatible with capacitor, tauri, or electron? yes, via the platform adapter system. override individual sub-ports without rebuilding the entire bundle: the player's core logic only calls the interfaces, it does not import capacitor or tauri directly. where do i report bugs? - nomercy-video-player: github.com/nomercy-entertainment/nomercy-video-player/issues - nomercy-music-player: github.com/nomercy-entertainment/nomercy-music-player/issues - nomercy-player-core: github.com/nomercy-entertainment/nomercy-player-core/issues

title: Migration Guide: v1 to v2

event payload extensibility: v1 events carried raw objects and multi-field flat structs. v2 wraps everything: instead of raw , instead of the item alone. adding a field to a v2 event is non-breaking; it was breaking in v1. - overloaded getter/setter pattern: reads, writes. eliminates / pairs. - plugin system replacement: v1 used . v2 uses . class-based plugins enable typescript inference, tree-shaking, and typed cross-plugin events. - opt-in features: eq, spectrum, mediasession, auto-advance were always-on in v1. in v2, they are opt-in plugins. zero cost if you don't add them. the top five breaks these affect every v1 consumer: 1. all event payloads changed every call needs updating. examples: 2. / → > this is the silent-break risk. the player will load without error but fail to play anything. music player: → video player: → map the field in your adapter layer: the server api should be updated to emit directly. 3. plugin api replaced 4. methods renamed | v1 | v2 | | -------------------- | ------------------------ | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | event | event | | event video | event | 5. always-on features are now opt-in plugins string → number video v1 was a formatted string like . v2 is a number in seconds. formatters that expected a string will produce . update any component that displays or compares duration: event timing v1 music player fired after a hardcoded delay. v2 fires after setup and all plugins resolve. do not rely on timing, always . what's new in v2 v2 ships features that did not exist in v1: - title: Player Core
description: The shared engine under both the video and music players. Adapter ports for every cross-cutting concern, a typed event bus, lifecycle machine, auth pipeline, plugin system, i18n, and storage.
content: nomercy-player-core is the package the video and music players are built from. you rarely install it yourself; pull in either library and the core comes along as a dependency. it carries everything that has nothing to do with video or audio in particular: the queue, the auth pipeline, the plugin system, the typed event bus, i18n, storage, and an adapter port for every cross-cutting concern. those parts are the same whether you are playing a film or an album, so they live here once instead of twice, and a fix to any of them reaches both players at the same time. you do not run the core on its own. it is the substrate the library packages stand on. what the core provides - lifecycle machine: 13-phase state machine from through to - plugin system: typed base class, dependency resolution, error quarantine, recovery policy - event bus: typed , cancellable events, cross-plugin event routing - auth pipeline: bearer token injection, 401 refresh, 403 propagation - queue engine: append, prepend, remove, move, sort, shuffle, backlog - i18n: adapter, method, async language loading - storage: adapter with , , - metrics: shape, , throttled event - adapter ports: pluggable interfaces for every cross-cutting concern when to depend on the core directly most consumers install or . both packages re-export the core's public api. install directly only if you: - are writing a library-level plugin that must work with both video and music players without importing either - are building a new library package on top of the core core sections | topic | page | | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | | the adapter ports | adapters | | built-in plugins shipped with the core | plugins | | typed event system, on/once/off/emit | event system | | 13-phase lifecycle machine | lifecycle | | auth fetch, 401/403, retry | auth & fetch | | i18n adapter and vite plugin | i18n | | error codes, notimplementederror, catch patterns | errors | | playbackmetrics, null-when-unavailable matrix | metrics | | testing subpath stub player | testing | architecture context the core owns nothing above layer 2. it does not import from the library packages and has no knowledge of or .

title: What is the Video Player
description: The headless web video player as an empty shell: it mounts into your element, plays standard video plus HLS, reflects state as CSS classes, and drives everything through events, methods, and swappable building blocks.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player-v2/src/index.ts, packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/core/mixins/container-class-emit.ts, lifecycle.ts / what is the nomercy video player is the headless web video player that powers video on nomercy tv. it plays standard video through the browser's native element and adds adaptive streaming over hls, and because the playback backend is a swappable adapter, other streaming formats plug in the same way. it also handles the genuinely hard parts for you matching hdr to the display, rendering subtitles in several formats, switching bitrate as the network shifts on an adaptive stream and then gets out of your way. the important word is headless. there is no ui in the box and no layout you have to accept. what you get is a working video pipeline wired to plain events, plain methods, and a set of building blocks you can swap. everything you see on screen is yours to build, or you bring in the optional and start from a finished one. the choice stays with you. an empty shell you drive think of the player as an empty shell with three ways in: - methods are how you tell it what to do: , , , to seek, . - events are how it tells you what happened: , , , , , and the rest of a fully typed event map. - adapters are the fundamental behaviors you can exchange: the playback backend, the thumbnail, chapter, and subtitle sources, storage, the event bus, the clock, and the url resolver. each one has a sensible default and a port you can replace without subclassing anything. nothing is hidden behind a ui you cannot reach. if the player can do it, there is a method, an event, or an adapter for it. what it does to your page you give the player an element. it mounts into that element in place, it does not wrap it or replace it. after , your own element is the player container. the player adds the class your existing classes and styles stay, appends a child, and from then on keeps the element in sync with playback: state classes you can use or ignore as playback changes, the player reflects state as css classes on your container. you never have to read them, but they are there the moment you want to style around state without writing a single event listener. the play state is one of , , , , , or mutually exclusive. on top of that it toggles , , , and , and it flips / as the viewer moves the pointer or goes idle. this is the complete set. every class below is added and removed for you by the core as events fire, so this table is the one place you need: | class | on the container while | group | | --- | --- | --- | | | media is playing | play state one at a time | | | playback is paused, and as the initial resting state | play state | | | playback has been stopped | play state | | | playback reached the end | play state | | | a source is loading | play state | | | playback stalled waiting for data | play state | | | audio is muted | independent toggle | | | the player is in fullscreen | independent toggle | | | the player is in picture-in-picture | independent toggle | | | theater mode is on | independent toggle | | | the viewer moved the pointer recently | activity paired | | | the viewer has gone idle | activity paired | the six play-state classes are mutually exclusive: the container always carries exactly one. the four toggles are independent and can stack. and are a pair, exactly one at a time. use them to drive an entire ui from css, mix them with event listeners, or ignore them completely and style nothing. they are an affordance, never a requirement. driven by events and methods because the player is event and api driven, your ui is just a listener on one side and a caller on the other. this is the whole pattern: there is no template to fight and no markup you have to match. react to what you care about, drive what you need, and leave the rest. swappable building blocks the defaults are good, but none of them are locked in. each fundamental behavior is an adapter port you can replace with your own: - swap the backend to drive a different media element or a non-hls source. - swap the thumbnail, chapter, or subtitle source to read your own formats. - swap storage to persist preferences server-side instead of in the browser. - swap the event bus, clock, or url resolver when you need to integrate with an existing system or test in isolation. that is the door this design opens: a working engine you can reshape from the outside, so the player bends to your product instead of your product bending to the player. where it sits the generic parts queue, auth, plugins, i18n, storage live in underneath, so this package stays focused on the hard video parts. plugin authors type against rather than the concrete class. .' , n: 1, name: 'nomercy-player-core', pkg: 'dependency', knows: 'queue, auth, plugins, event bus, i18n, storage.' , /> start here - installation: add the package, npm or cdn - quick start: a working player in a few lines - configuration: every multi-language audio pass subtitle tracks per playlist item: for ass/ssa subtitles with full typesetting, add from the subpath, see plugins: octopus. cdn embed no bundler the iife bundle exposes a one paragraph the player is headless: a pure typescript engine with no built-in ui. it manages the hls pipeline, queue, tracks, auth, and state, and communicates through typed events and css classes on the container element. everything on screen is a plugin — is the first-party overlay; replace it, extend it, or build your own. all plugins share the same lifecycle. they are registered via before helpers keep elements scoped to the player container and give the plugin system a clean reference to tear them down. the three you will use most often: reacting to state the player applies css classes steps, the source lives at . tutorial steps | step | what you build | | --- | --- | | 1: plugin shell and layout | base plugin class, container layout, css structure | | 2: play, pause, and buffering | center play button, buffering spinner, click-to-toggle | | 3: progress bar with seeking | seekable slider, buffer bar, hover preview time | | 4: time display and skip buttons | current time, duration, 10 s skip forward and back | | 5: volume control | mute toggle, volume slider, icon state | | 6: top bar with title | episode or movie title overlay | | 7: fullscreen and playback speed | complete three-zone overlay, responds to every playback state transition, exposes seek and volume controls, renders a sprite-thumbnail tooltip on hover, and handles touch input with double-tap seek content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player-v2/wiki/guides/step-10-touch-zones.md / step 10: touch zones this is the final step of the "build a player ui" tutorial. you will add a transparent touch/click zone overlay to that handles double-tap to seek backward and forward, single-tap to toggle controls visibility, center double-tap for fullscreen, and, on mobile, top/bottom center zones for volume. this is the pattern the built-in uses. you are building it from scratch here to understand how it works. if you want the ready-made version, register directly and skip this step, see touch zones plugin. what you are building the overlay is a 3-column, 6-row css grid that covers the entire player container. on desktop the three columns span the full height. on mobile, the center column splits into three rows for volume up, play/pause, and volume down. | zone | single tap | double tap | | ---- | ---------- | ---------- | | left | hide controls if visible | seek back | | right | hide controls if visible | seek forward | | center desktop | toggle play/pause | toggle fullscreen | | center mobile | toggle play/pause if controls shown | toggle fullscreen | | vol up mobile | hide controls if visible | | | vol down mobile | hide controls if visible | | plugin scaffold this step uses the same class you have been building throughout the tutorial. the class shape stays the same: , a method, and a . inject the css the overlay relies on a small amount of css. inject it once when runs rather than bundling a separate stylesheet. the guard prevents duplicate injection when multiple player instances share a page. > tailwind note: the tutorial uses utility classes elsewhere in the series for control bar elements. css is used here instead because grid-area assignments and layering need to be precise and are easier to verify when they are not mixed with utility classes. substitute tailwind if your project uses it. double-tap detection the core utility for this step is a function that returns an event handler distinguishing single-tap from double-tap. two taps within milliseconds trigger the double-tap callback; a tap that arrives after the threshold fires the single-tap callback. the threshold is configurable so your plugin can expose it as an option, matching 's option. building the grid overlay add and call it from . the method creates the root grid div, appends it to the player container, detects touch capability, and places the appropriate zones. the and strings are css grid-column and grid-row shorthand values assigned directly on each zone element. tracking controls visibility the zones need to know whether the controls overlay is currently visible so that single-tap can conditionally hide it. the event is how broadcasts its show/hide state. wire it up in with a short debounce so that a tap that just woke the controls does not immediately re-hide them on the click that follows the touchstart. from the base class auto-unsubscribes on . do not use directly. zone box factory a helper that creates a positioned grid cell div: seek feedback indicator each seek zone gets a floating circular indicator that shows the accumulated seek time for the current tap burst. it is lazy-created on the first double-tap and lives in the dom for the plugin's lifetime. seek zones is the base class helper. it registers the event listener and removes it automatically on . never use directly, as that bypasses the lifecycle registry and leaks on teardown. playback zone the center zone toggles play/pause on single-tap and fullscreen on double-tap. on desktop the single-tap always fires; on mobile it only fires when controls are already visible the first tap wakes the overlay via the container's own touchstart, not this zone. volume zones mobile not a plugin-scoped event. would send , which nothing listens to. only needs to remove the grid root from the dom. listeners registered through and are already removed by the lifecycle registry before title: Framework: Angular

content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player-v2/wiki/frameworks/framework-angular.md / video player: angular integration afterviewinit / ondestroy pattern the player requires a real dom element before it can mount, so initialization belongs in , not in the constructor or . clean up with in to release the hls instance and all event listeners. do not store the player in an angular signal or a directly. the player is a class instance with a rich internal state tree, and reactive wrappers will try to observe its properties, which causes interference. keep the reference as a plain class field and push only primitive state values into observables. using the component pass a from the parent component. use together with relative paths on each playlist item so the same config works across environments without string concatenation. service pattern: shared player state across components when several components need to read or control the same player, an angular service is the right place to own the instance. expose primitive state as observables so components can subscribe with the pipe or . consuming the service in a component the player container component initializes the service. other components, such as a transport bar, inject the same service and subscribe to the observables. auth-protected streams pass the object in the config when your hls manifests and segments require a bearer token. on 401, fires once and the request is retried automatically. 403 propagates and is not retried. what to read next - configuration: every config option and default - api methods: full method reference - events: all events and payload shapes - plugin development: writing your own plugins - framework: vue: vue 3 composable pattern - framework: react: react useref pattern

content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player-v2/wiki/frameworks/framework-vanilla.md / video player: vanilla js no framework is required to use the player. you can load it from a cdn with a single tag, or import it directly in any bundler-based project vite, rollup, webpack, esbuild. cdn / script-tag path load first, then the player iife bundle. the bundle reads from , so the order matters. is the factory function exposed by the iife bundle. pass it the of your container element and chain . > note: built-in plugins such as are not included in the iife bundle. to use them you need the esm path with a bundler, described in the next section. bundler / esm path install the package see installation, then import and initialize after the dom is ready: accepts a plugin class, not an instance. chain as many plugins as you need before calling . wiring transport controls once you have a player instance, any dom button or keyboard listener can call methods directly: all player methods are synchronous reads or async commands. you never need to mutate internal state directly. auth-protected streams pass an object in the config to add a token to every hls manifest and segment request: on a 401, fires once and the failed request is retried. a 403 propagates without a retry. cleanup call when you remove the player from the page. it tears down the backend, releases the hls instance, and cleans up all event listeners: if you are building a single-page app without a framework, wire this to whatever signals the player is leaving the view, for example a route change callback or a watching the container element: what to read next - quick start: the first working player in under a minute - configuration: every config option and default - api methods: full method reference - events: all events and their payload shapes - plugins: desktop ui: the built-in controls overlay - plugin development: writing your own plugins
